Mr. Speaker, in view of the finance minister's statement a few moments ago that the income restraint program should be borne equally by all segments of the economy, I

want to ask him what restraints will be placed on corporation dividends in view of the fact that the proposal which the minister has sent out definitely excludes corporation dividends on the ground that "the disposition of profits is better left to the companies so that they may feel freer to determine how best to raise their capital". subtopic: INFLATION-APPLICABILITY OF RESTRAINT PROGRAM TO CORPORATE DIVIDENDS

There are no clear answers to that, but that certainly is a subject which is open for discussion.

speakeroldname: Hon. James Hugh Faulkner (Secretary of State):
subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in introducing Bill C-58 at second reading I should like to sketch in some of the background to this legislation. It seems to me it is a fact that in any free society, magazines significantly influence the development of the culture, the national sensibility, the free play of ideas and exchange of views and the critical faculties of its citizens. One might say that the part magazines play in this process is perhaps not as directly influential as television or films, but that may be largely a matter of taste and circumstances. Certainly, if one can judge by the views expressed by hundreds of persons who have written to me during the past few months about possible changes in the income tax law affecting advertising in periodicals, magazines are a very important factor indeed in terms of developing and nurturing a distinctly Canadian culture and identity.
During the past quarter-century, several royal commissions and special committees, charged by the Canadian government with looking into matters relating to the survival of a Canadian culture, have held in common the belief that the capacity and capability of Canadian periodicals to support the writing and exchange of ideas was of great importance and ought to be strengthened and supported by government assistance and intervention where and when appropriate. In the words of the Massey commission report:
The periodical press of Canada ... does undoubtedly make a conscious, and it seems to us, a successful appeal to the country as a whole ... We do have ... a periodical press which ... insists on remaining resolutely Canadian.
The report, in 1961, of the royal commission headed by a distinguished Canadian, Grattan O'Leary, stated that the role of the periodical press in building Canadian unity cannot be ignored. It said:
Periodicals educate, inform, entertain, and amuse. They provide the forum for debate and discussion which is essential to the democratic process.
It added that the problems besetting the Canadian periodical press affect its ability to add to "the richness and variety of Canadian life." To attain self-sufficiency, the O'Leary report stated, Canadian periodicals required adequate advertising revenue, and it concluded:
A nation's domestic advertising expenditure should be devoted to the support of its own media of communications, and ... a genuinely Canadian periodical press can only exist if it has access to a fair share of advertising revenue.
More recently, the Davey committee suggested that "in terms of cultural survival, magazines could potentially be as important as railroads, airlines, national broadcasting networks and national hockey leagues." It recommended that the benefits enjoyed by such foreign-owned periodicals as Time and Reader's Digest under the special exemption provision in section 19 of the Income Tax Act be withdrawn. Now, some years later, this government is asking parliament to give effect to the views and recommendations of this trio of learned and significant reports.

Mr. Speaker, this is an important bill and an important debate. Our discussion in the House will focus attention upon and enhance public understanding of a very significant section of our society, the Canadian periodical industry, and could affect significantly the future role, direction and prosperity of that industry. The difficulties facing that industry have for some time been a matter of concern to my department and to me; for some months now we have been engaged, in co-operation with the industry, in the development of a plan of action aimed at finding solutions to certain of its problems. I regard the amendment proposed in this bill as an important element of that plan and one that is essential to its success.
The government's intention to seek an amendment to section 19 of the Income Tax Act respecting foreign-owned periodicals has been termed by some critics a negative decision. I submit that it is not a negative decision if its succeeds in eliminating a situation which for years has had a negative effect on a very large part of the Canadian-owned periodical press in this country. It is not a negative decision if it leads to positive results; when it is seen as a stage in the development of a program of effective government assistance to Canadian periodicals about which I shall be speaking a little later.
It is probably trite to say that the government did not arrive easily at this decision. Throughout the course of our deliberations my colleagues and I have been conscious of the implications of the proposed measure for those magazines affected. But the arguments, as we saw them, outweighed those other considerations, arguments that took into account the inequities of the situation preserved by the existing legislation, and the intangible but no less real factors of cultural integrity and the preservation and growth of an indispensable medium of expression of Canadian ideas, sentiments and values.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
It may sound like it, but I suggest the hon. member read the bill. The approval which my statement in the House on January 23 received from all parties, and the public approval as evidenced by press commentary and by the volume of favourable messages I have received, leave no doubt that in the minds of the majority of Canadians the government's decision was well taken.
In taking the decision, the government-and I dare say this parliament-is declaring what it is we do not want. First, we do not want the continuance of a special case provision in the Income Tax Act the justification for which, whatever it might have been when it was introduced ten years ago, no longer exists and which is inconsistent with the intent of section 19; a provision which not only discriminates in favour of a handful of Canadian-based, foreign-owned magazines against a very large number of foreign magazines circulating in Canada but, much more seriously, gives a very inequitable advantage to those few magazines over Canadian-owned periodicals.
May 8, 1975

Second, we do not want the continuance of an arrangement whereby two very large, foreign-owned periodicals- one with a weekly circulation of 1.4 million-together drew off $19 million of the $39 million of advertising revenue earned in 1974 by the 13 largest consumer magazines in Canada.
Third, we do not want the continuance of a situation wherein the world view of Canadian readers is being influenced by American periodicals the operations of which in Canada are facilitated by a tax deduction provision primarily intended to assist Canadian publications.
Fourth, we do not want the continuance of a practice whereby the stories and articles reproduced in the French language Canadian edition of Reader's Digest are usually translated outside Canada.
Fifth, we do not want the continuance of an arrangement whereby the editorial content of these foreign-owned magazines is imported from parent houses in the United States, which have already paid for it from large advertising and circulation revenues in that country, at a cost that is negligible by comparison with what it costs Canadian-owned magazines to produce their editorial content.
Sixth, we do not want the continuance, on the part of two foreign-owned magazines, of editorial policies that can hardly be said to be making a real contribution to Canadian cultural development and expression.
Seventh, we do not want the continuance of a situation wherein foreign-owned magazines claim the right to be called Canadian while taking their editorial direction and most of their editorial content from their parent houses abroad.
Eighth, we do not want the continuance of a Canadiani-zation progress record which, after thirty years, finds Time in Canada still owned and controlled entirely by Time Inc. in the United States and publishing perhaps 10 per cent Canadian content; and Reader's Digest only 30 per cent Canadian-owned and carrying in its English language edition about 25 per cent and, in its French language edition, about 15 per cent Canadian content.
What we do want is: first, the continuance of a situation wherein there is no interference with the freedom of Canadians to read Time and Reader's Digest, the foreign editions of which, should the owners choose to cease publishing in Canada, would still be able to enter and circulate freely in Canada in the same way as a multitude of other periodicals of foreign origin. In this respect, whatever may be the decision of the owners regarding publishing editions in Canada, we would expect that it would continue to be seen as being to their advantage to have their magazines printed in this country and distributed by the Canadian postal service.
Second, we want the diversion of a proportion of the advertising revenue now earned by Time and Reader's Digest to Canadian-owned consumer magazines.
Third we want the emergence of a Canadian weekly news magazine, or magazines, designed to meet the needs and tastes of Canadians in both official languages.
Fourth, encouraged by improved competitive conditions in the market, we want an increase in the size, number

and saleability of Canadian magazines and resultant enlarged opportunities for Canadian writers and readers.
Those, Mr. Speaker, are the main things we would like to see come about as a result of this proposed legislation. I, personally, am confident we shall see them. In the Speech from the Throne on September 30, 1974, this government said it would be taking further steps to enchance Canada's independence and sense of identity, among other ways, by promoting the sale of Canadian books and magazines. The bill now before hon. members proposes a considerable measure of assistance in that respect where Canadian magazines are concerned. At Trent University last January, in an address to the conference on the state of English language publishing in Canada, I outlined a series of other measures the government intends to take to enhance the capability of Canadian magazines to develop and prosper and to compete successfully in the home market. I talked of a program of assistance, not through hand-outs but by financial contributions aimed at enabling magazine publishers to help themselves.
I emphasized the government's willingness to support co-operative and collective self-help projects of Canadian magazine publishers, especially the class of smaller, paid circulation magazines which speak to and for Canadians about Canada and Canadian issues and interests and which survive because of their combined appeal to both readers and advertisers but only with great difficulty in the face of tough competition from imported publications.
I announced that beginning in fiscal year 1975-76, the Canada Council would be extending its already substantial assistance to literary and arts magazines and to other magazines of a more varied nature to help them with co-operative endeavours to strengthen their competitive capability. I said that I saw additional resources being directed by Canada Council to finance projects proposed by the publishers through their representative associations and aimed at improving the promotion, distribution and marketing of Canadian periodicals as well as in achieving a higher level of management skill. The Canada Council now has this program in hand.
I spoke of the government's willingness to give financial assistance to the development of a common national distribution service designed to get Canadian periodicals into outlets in communities where they are rarely, if ever, accessible to Canadian readers at the present time, I am glad to report that proposals for such a service have been developed by groups representative of the periodical industry and these proposals will soon be ready for discussion with my department and other government agencies. I said that we are consulting with other federal departments concerned with a view to providing greater display space for Canadian periodicals on newsstands and book-stalls operating on federal government facilities such as airports and railway stations. We are considering schemes for using federal government buildings in towns and cities across the country for displaying and promoting Canadian publications.
We are examining the possibility of increasing the amount of space purchased by government departments and agencies in Canadian periodicals, to increase the

May 8, 1975

awareness of Canadians with regard to programs and activities of those departments and agencies. Interdepartmental consultations at the official level are now going on with that end in view.
These are some of the plans we have for extending assistance to the periodical industry. The magazine associations have recommended additional courses of action and we have them under careful consideration. The measure before us today will help to ensure that these proposals for support to Canadian magazine publishers achieve the desired results by creating an environment that is more conducive to competition on fairer terms than now prevail.
No government, and certainly not this one, is interested in underwriting mediocrity. It has no intention of using taxpayers' dollars to help create an environment wherein a magazine is able to keep on publishing, shielded from the rigours of the marketplace, simply because it is Canadian, a container of Canadian culture and a reflector of Canadian identity in one or other of the many forms in which those concepts tend to be manifest. We are not concerned with making the marketplace safe for Canadian magazines. We are prepared to do what we can to make it fair and to help those Canadian magazines which have shown by their performance that they are deserving of a fighting chance.
It will be up to Canadian readers to decide whether a particular Canadian magazine shall survive, because it is their newsstand purchasers and their subscriptions which alone will decide what amount of available advertising dollars will be attracted to it. As with any product, quality and customer acceptance are the essential ingredients for success. Where they are present in a magazine, the assistance it will need from government will be minimal. Magazine publishers know this to be the government's stand in respect of financial support, and most of them endorse it.
I said at Trent University and earlier in my remarks today that I was hopeful that one of the results of the proposed changes in the income tax law would be the emergence of a Canadian magazine. Canadian readers are entitled to a news magazine which will report both national and international events in a manner which makes them relevant and significant to Canada and Canadians. A "window on the world through American-tinted glass", as Senator Keith Davey aptly put it recently, is not a satisfactory function of a news magazine where Canadians are concerned, regardless of how clearly and colourfully those events may be presented.
I have reason to believe that more than one Canadian publisher is interested in starting a weekly magazine, and indeed one at least is on record as saying it will start one if the changes in the Income Tax Act are made. It will be our hope that such a magazine, besides informing its readers on major events and issues on the international scene would, while dealing with current topics of national concern, give special and adequate attention to matters of regional significance and interest.
A leading Canadian advertising agency stated recently that there is no guarantee that the so-called expulsion of the domestic editions of Time and Reader's Digest will allow the introduction of a new Canadian news magazine. I agree with this statement; there is no such guarantee. All

this government can expect from the proposed changes in the tax law is a situation to be brought about wherein a Canadian news magazine, as well as other consumer magazines, will have a better chance to get started and to keep going once they are under way.
Concern has been expressed in some quarters over what is expected of publishers in terms of the amount of so-called Canadian content a periodical must contain in order to be classified as a Canadian periodical for the purposes of the Income Tax Act. I should like to make it quite clear that there is no intention of introducing, in connection with the proposed amendments, a new Canadian content rule or a new formula for measuring how substantially a magazine published in Canada must be different from another published abroad in order to qualify for the benefits of section 19 of the Income Tax Act. Such a criterion has been part of the taxation law since 1965; it is not new and it is not unique. All periodicals published in Canada are bound by the "not substantially the same" clause in section 19 and have been for nearly ten years.
What is new is that for the first time certain periodicals being published in Canada and which are now foreign owned, if they decide to become Canadianized through transfer of ownership and control will, at the same time, like their fellow Canadian magazines, have to abide by the "not substantially the same" clause if they expect to benefit from the provisions of section 19. It is as simple as that. It may not seem simple from the standpoint of the publishers of those magazines, but the requirement is clear and has been clearly stated in the law since 1965. Nothing would be changed except the extent of its application.
There need be no mystery or uncertainty as to how this clause is to be interpreted and administered. Administrators of the Income Tax Act are called upon daily for such interpretations and administrative decisions in respect of many sections of the act, and in the case of dissatisfaction on the part of a taxpayer with an interpretation or decision, there is a well established process of appeal to the courts. In the case of uncertainty in the mind of any publisher contemplating the publication in Canada of a periodical with a certain format and editiorial content, it is possible, I am assured by my colleague the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford), to obtain an advance ruling from his department on the eligibility of that periodical for the benefits under section 19.
What some persons are calling the new Canadian content requirement has nothing whatsoever to do with censorship, about which the hon. member for Calgary North (Mr. Woolliams) seems to be confused, or with government control over what Canadians may read. It in no way implies government interference with the editorial policy of periodical publishers. It has to do with the application of those provisions of the existing law which define what makes a periodical a Canadian periodical and thereby entitled to the benefits of certain fiscal provisions, benefits intended for Canadian periodicals.
Contrary to the view expressed in a recent editorial in one of our leading financial journals, a periodical, to be counted for tax purposes as a Canadian publication, does not have to have a certain minimum percentage of Canadi-
May 8, 1975

an content. It should be understood by everyone that to be "not substantially the same" as a periodical printed, edited or published outside Canada does not mean that a magazine's contents have to be Canadian in whole or in part. They simply have to be such as to make that magazine, for the most part, different from a foreign counterpart. It is conceivable that a periodical published in Canada and which satisfied all the requirements of section 19 could be ruled to be a Canadian periodical even if it contained not a single article or story by a Canadian writer or about a Canadian subject. I say "conceivable" but, I am bound to say-and I am sure hon. members will agree-not desirable.
Section 19 of the Income Tax Act is not aimed directly or primarily at encouraging Canadian authorship, although one might reasonably expect it to have that effect. Its purpose, in particular the "not substantially the same" provision, is essentially to help Canadian periodical publishers to counterbalance undue foreign competition caused by the dumping of editorial material prepared outside our country and reproduced virtually unchanged in so-called Canadian editions. This is editorial material the cost of which is already amortized abroad before it is supplied to so-called Canadian editions at a fraction of what it would cost a Canadian-owned magazine to prepare and publish comparable material. The editorial I have referred to went on to ask:
What gives Ottawa the idea that it has the right to determine what shall and what shall not be printed in Canadian publications?

As I suggested, Mr. Speaker, it is anticipated, and with justification, I submit, that Canadian authors, journalists and commentators will benefit from this amendment. We believe that Canadian periodicals now in print, as well as others that we hope will emerge in time, will attract a growing number of Canadian staff writers and contributors. We look for the appearance of new Canadian periodicals that will address themselves to subject matters of major interest to Canadian readers and will give expression to the Canadian point of view. But it is precisely because this government and this House believe in the freedom of Canadians to choose what they wish to read that neither is about to direct publishers of magazines, or of any other kind of publication, how they should discharge their responsibility to serve the Canadian community and the Canadian purpose, culturally or in any other way.
Then, Mr. Speaker, there is in addition the question of producing or publishing a periodical in Canada under licence from someone abroad. But this is largely a matter of the facts of the contractual agreement that exists between the two parties and should not be a cause for uncertainty in the mind of a publisher. Again, I would expect that Revenue Canada officials can be helpful in advising a publisher of his position as regards that aspect of the act. The provision on licensing has been law since 1965.
Mr. Speaker, I spoke earlier of the importance the government attaches to this measure. It is important because the growth and prosperity of a periodical industry are important to any country that wishes to preserve and reinforce its identity and the special character of its society and culture. It is a natural and laudable desire for a country to favour its own publications to the fullest possible extent but within reason and with equity. Canadian magazine publishers have been forced to exist for too long in an economic and psychological climate that has not been conducive to growth or new ventures. We want to see that climate changed, and the measures now before this House is, in our judgment, designed to help that change take place. We want to see a better economic environment for magazines edited by and for Canadians, with a Canadian point of view. Whether they make the grade with Canadian readers will depend upon the free choice of Canadians. Influencing that choice in their favour remains the task and the challenge of Canadian magazine publishers.
If, as I said at the beginning, periodicals significantly influence the development and expression of a country's culture and identity, it seems to follow that if this influence emanates in very large part from periodicals of foreign origin or under foreign control, such development and expressions are unlikely to take a form or direction that is desirable from the point of view of most Canadians. In so far as the outlook of Canadians is shaped largely by what they find in American magazines, this is not to be critical of what may be called the American world-view; it is simply to point out that it is not ours and should not be. Many Canadians are often better informed on United States politics and affairs than on those of their own country.

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
The contribution of Canadian magazines to the enhancement of Canadian cultural expression, to the articulation of Canadian issues and to the knowledge and understanding of Canadians of their own country and their fellow Canadians is overshadowed by that of American publications. Surely, ways have to be found to redress the balance, and by that I do not mean ways that entail interference with the free flow into Canada of periodicals published abroad. The erection of cultural barriers or hidden tariffs has no part in what we are trying to achieve through measures to assist Canadian magazine publishing.
If Canadian readership patterns are to be changed in respect of magazines, so that Canadian magazines have a fairer chance to influence Canadian cultural growth and the expression and diffusion of Canadian ideas and creativity, Canadian magazines must come to be of such quality and so varied in content as to offer Canadians acceptable substitutes for the numerous choices of foreign-owned publications now available throughout the country. This transformation-and it can hardly be called less than a transformation-has got to be the absolutely top priority for magazine publishers in this country in the years to come if there is to continue to be any validity in the claim that Canadian periodicals are important to our culture.
As the minister responsible for federal government policy and programs aimed at the betterment of cultural and artistic activity and achievement, I have an obligation to see to it that Canadian periodical publishers who address their efforts determinedly and vigorously to this priority get all the support and assistance it is practicable and appropriate for the Canadian government to extend to them.

Mr. Speaker, in the absence of my colleague, the Minister of Communications (Mr. Pelletier), I would now like to refer to the various aspects of the bill which deal with broadcasting. The clauses dealing with advertizing broadcasted by foreign stations are generally similar to the above-mentioned clauses on periodicals and newspapers. The aims are the same, that is to strengthen and promote the development of Canadian media by improving their profitability.
The advertising market for Canadian viewers is operated through American border stations. There are about a dozen American television stations located close to the Canadian border whose programs are seen by a great number of Canadians either directly or through cablevi-sion. Those stations have reaped substantial advertising revenues in Canadian towns where their programs are widely seen. Indeed, the very existence of some of those stations is based on advertising made in Canada.
According to present estimates, some $20 million are paid each year out of Canada to those American stations for advertising directed to Canadian viewers. From that yearly amount of $20 million, some $9 million come from the television market in the Toronto area and some $7 million from Vancouver. Southern Manitoba loses about $1.5 million each year to American stations. The remainder comes from Ottawa, Montreal and a few other smaller markets.
Most of the American stations involved, especially those situated in Buffalo (N.Y.) in Pembina (North Dakota), in Bellingham (Washington) are actively canvassing advertising accounts with Canada companies who wish to sell their products to Canadians. It can be safely stated, Mr. Speaker, that some stations have been created for the sole purpose of tapping the Canadian market.
The economic exploitation of the Canadian advertising market has important consequences for our broadcasting system. The licensing policy of the Canadian RadioTelevision Commission is based on the ability of each local market to support with advertising revenues the Canadian stations licensed to serve it. Clearly, when revenues which would otherwise go to local Canadian stations are siphoned off to United States border stations, the CRTC's licensing policy is undermined. The Broadcasting Act passed by this House in 1968 states:
-the Canadian broadcasting system should be effectively owned and controlled by Canadians so as to safeguard, enrich and strengthen the cultural, political, social and economic fabric of Canada-
One of the objectives this government has pursued in the development of communications policy is that Canadians should have access to as wide a choice of information and entertainment as possible and Canadian sources of creativity and information should be emphasized. We are confident that this measure will not in any way limit the choice of programming available to Canadians. However, uncontrolled siphoning off of advertising revenues adversely affects the financial viability of many Canadian stations. Affected, as well, is the ability of Canadian stations to assume greater and more costly policy obligations such as local program production. Moreover, the loss of revenues to United States border stations threatens to hinder the expansion of the Canadian broadcasting system by reducing the amount of money available to provide service to the smaller areas where the markets are not large enough themselves to support a private broadcasting operation.
The objective of this bill is to create a financial incentive which would encourage the repatriation of Canadian advertising dollars. By taking away the privilege of deductions against income of the costs of advertising broadcast on non-Canadian stations, the bill will effectively double the cost of advertising time on the United States stations. This will not eliminate all advertising on United States border stations, but it will become more attractive to purchase time on Canadian stations. In this way, the bill will contribute to the reversal of the outflow of Canadian advertising revenues. Not only will the viability and integrity of Canadian broadcasting stations be enhanced, but the development of the Canadian broadcasting system will also be assisted.
In other words, Mr. Speaker, while it is difficult to predict the amount of funds that will be diverted to the Canadian broadcasting system, more funds will become available to assist in extending the coverage of the Canadian broadcasting system to more Canadians, and more money will be available to assist the development of Canadian sources of creativity. To prevent the harm

May 8, 1975

which could befall Canadian advertisers if the deductions were removed before adequate alternative time was available on Canadian stations, the provisions of the bill dealing with broadcast advertising will not be implemented until adequate time is available. Of the two markets which were previously fully bought up, southern Ontario and Vancouver, the former, southern Ontario, has seen the recent licensing of both the Global television network and channel 79. Consequently, Canadian advertising time is available in that area now.
In the Vancouver area, it is expected that a third television station will be licensed in the near future by the Canadian Radio-Television Commission, thus ensuring that advertisers in that area are able to buy Canadian advertising time. It is proposed that the implementation of this bill should take into account the timing of the licensing of this third Vancouver station. To that end, those parts of the bill relating to broadcasting will be put into effect by proclamation. There may, therefore, be a delay between the enactment of the bill and the proclamation of the broadcasting clause in order to allow the establishment of the third Vancouver station.

This legislation will amend the Income Tax Act so as to encourage the return of Canadian advertising revenues to the Canadian broadcasting companies just as we have done up to now and as we will keep on doing regarding the fourth estate. This amendment has been supported by the CRTC, the Standing Committee on Broadcasting, Films and Assistance to the Arts, the Special Senate Committee on Mass Media and by all the representatives of the Canadian broadcasting industry. It is part and parcel of the government's endeavour to maintain in Canada a wholesome and strong broadcasting system.

Mr. Speaker, the support which the proposed legislation will provide to the Canadian periodical industry and to the Canadian broadcasting system manifests the determination of this government to encourage all areas of cultural expression. The government has the duty to ensure that the imagination and talent of Canadians be given room to develop and to grow. The measures we are proposing here today are an important step toward that goal.

Mr. Speaker, I went to some length in trying to point out to the hon. member and the House that this bill does not deal with the concept of Canadian content. It deals with the concept of "not substantially the same," a provision which has been in the act since 1965 and concerns material edited abroad, no matter where, placed in so-called Canadian editions and passed off as Canadian. The bill does not deal with the concept of Canadian content. I went to some length in attempting to clear up that misconception. Obviously, I did not do it to the satisfaction of the hon. member, but I will do so in committee.

Mr. Speaker, the report of the Royal Commission on Publications dated May, 1961, emphasized that in an area as vital and as sensitive as the press, whatever is done should be positive rather than negative, with the goal being the promotion of the Canadian periodical and not the suppression of the foreign periodical. That is the theme I want to develop this afternoon. I shall raise some points which the minister obviously overlooked.
Although the minister made a most interesting speech, the amendments he proposes to the Income Tax Act as put forward in Bill C-58 in no way constitute a periodicals policy for Canada. I think, personally, and I hope most will agree, that is wrong of a tax policy to differentiate with respect to, say, Time and Reader's Digest as this leads to all sorts of anomalies and possibly unfairness. A tax policy should apply equally. Time and Reader's Digest could easily fulfil their obligations as Canadian citizens by broadening substantially, over an agreed span of time, their Canadian ownership.
If I may draw an analogy, I suggest that both these magazines have been in Canada long enough to apply for Canadian citizenship. Perhaps application for citizenship could take the form of an increased sale of their shares to citizens of this country. Other acts, be they with respect to newspapers, banks or whatever, have demonstrated that this can be done if a reasonable length of time is permitted. I think the Bank Act provides for a period of five years, although I have not directed my mind to the exact length of time. In any event, there could be a time-frame in which publications could at the very least sell a majority of their shares to the citizens of this country.
The minister has admitted that the passage of this bill will not automatically mean the flow of revenue to Canadian magazines. As a matter of fact, an independent survey by Canadian Facts indicates that 19 to 20 per cent of the advertising revenue of Time and Reader's Digest will probably accrue to Canadian publications. When I had the privilege of meeting with the publisher and editor of the revitalized Saturday Night the other day, the question was posed to the publisher about the effect of Bill C-58. He admitted that from the point of view of policy, it would not be significant. Some of the other matters the minister mentioned, and some of the points I hope to develop, will have a much more significant effect on the future of Canadian publications.
As these magazines become Canadian citizens, it might be fair to ask that more of the decisions relative to their editorial content should be made in this country. The minister gave a somewhat lengthy exposition of the Canadian content rule. I am not convinced about this. Despite the fact that the legislation has been in place since, as the minister said, 1965, I hope the officials have made very few rulings. Perhaps the committee would be the place to learn just how many rulings have been made about content. My party and I are very nervous about this particular provision. I think that content rules, particularly as they have application to news magazines-here I am not making a plea for any magazine, but the whole concept of news magazines-are repellent to me and to this party.

The hon. member for Kingston and the Islands (Miss MacDonald) and several others are chastising me about that phrase. Anyway, there are enough editors of talent and writers of talent, be they men or women, to adequately provide content for any number of Canadian periodicals. That is not the problem. However, there is a very serious problem about management talent. I hope that in the development of a periodicals policy, some agency will assist. Also, I hope there will be a subsidy provision to provide for the training of managers of periodicals. Many knowledgeable people in the industry have told me that it is on the management side that the weakness lies.
There is, of course, the perennial problem of any artistic of cultural endeavour-the problem of money. I suppose, and I will develop this a little later, that the Canada Council or some organization along the lines of the Canadian Film Development Corporation could fulfil a useful function here. The last point-I am just highlighting at this stage-is that I was interested in the minister's comments about the distribution system. However, still he has done nothing more than make protestations about the need for an adequate distribution system.
When speaking at Trent University the Minister said that the strength, originality and vision of the Canadian publishing industry was not a matter of marginal interest or importance to the Liberal government but, rather, a true measure of what constitutes our national life. I like rhetoric as much as anybody else. At another time and in another place I would like to make a speech about the misuse of rhetoric, the raising of the expectations of people because of hyperbole when no firm policy follows the rhetoric.
The minister announced the government's intention to delete subsections (2) and (4) from section 19 of the Income Tax Act effective January, 1976, thereby eliminating the tax advantages currently enjoyed by the Canadian editions of Time and Reader's Digest. The minister stated, further, that the strength, originality and vision of the Canadian publishing industry was, as I said earlier, a matter of priority. I will suggest in the next few minutes that I would like to see substantially more evidence of the minister's concern. Similar sentiments about a periodical policy were expressed by the minister's predecessor in 1972. The then minister said the development of a Canadian publishing policy was a matter of top priority. Apparently "top priority" is nothing more than an empty phrase if Bill C-58 is the only evidence of the earnestness of the government in this regard.
In the minister's address to the Trent University conference on "The State of English Language Publishing in Canada", his sole commitment was to the amendment of the Income Tax Act. As I said earlier, a survey by Canadian Facts Incorporated, in January of this year, of Canadi-

an advertising executives indicated that the Canadian publishing industry will not benefit substantially from the removal of tax advantages for advertising in Time and Reader's Digest. As a matter of fact, the figure is only 19 or 20 per cent. However, there is a worrisome theme; it worried Senator Davey who headed the committee on publishing: only 19 per cent of the revenues freed by this measure will go to the publishing industry, and of that 19 per cent almost 60 per cent will go to Maclean-Hunter Publications. As a consequence, Maclean-Hunter will effectively control at least half of the advertising revenues obtained by the magazine industry. Little magazines will derive an almost insignificant amount of benefit from the legislation, despite the minister's admission that the smaller, special interest magazines constitute a real problem area, to use his words, in the publishing industry.
I began by referring to the report of the royal commission handed down in 1961 and its desire that legislation be positive. It seems to me that the legislation under debate today has been conceived along precisely opposite lines, that is to say, it would perform a negative function; it embodies a policy of negative, rather than positive assistance to an industry which, upon the hon. gentleman's own admission, is a true measure of what constitutes our national life. It would be more accurate to describe Bill C-58 as a true measure of the government's inability to meet the pressing problems of the Canadian industry and Canadian identity by not bringing forward concrete, positive policy commitments.
I intend to suggest a couple of positive commitments. The first has to do with postal rates and postal services. Because 91 per cent of Canadian magazine sales are through subscription, an efficient and economical postal service is of crucial importance to the survival of an indigenous periodical industry. Prior to 1968, the Post Office Act provided mailing rates for magazines of between 1 Vi cents and 3 cents a pound. The rate depended on circulation: periodicals with a circulation of less than
10.000	paid IV2 cents per pound; for a circulation between
10.000	and 50,000 the rate was 2 V2 cents per pound, and publications with a circulation of 50,000 or more paid 3 cents per pound.
However, the passage of Bill C-116 raised the price per pound from 3 cents to 5 cents and instituted a minimum floor rate of 2 cents per piece. Under such an arrangement, magazines with fewer pages, smaller size and consequently a lower volume of advertising are placed on the same footing as the larger, better financed periodicals. Similarly, the existence of the 2 cents per piece minimum charge has led to the establishment of independent distribution firms to distribute magazines which carry no price and which therefore concentrate heavily on advertising as a source of revenue. The growth of these controlled circulation publications has placed a serious drain on the pool of advertising revenues available in Canada.
Surely, a government which professes to be so keenly interested in encouraging the growth of the periodical industry would consider the removal of the floor charge of 2 cents, as advocated in the Davey committee report of 1970, in an attempt to restrain the controlled circulation section of the industry which it has fostered at the
May 8, 1975

expense of Canadian periodical sales. Canadian publishers consider that no other single action which the government could take would do as much to provide immediate relief and encouragement to those involved in this difficult and discouraging business. If the government's concern is to be considered sincere, positive steps must be taken to initiate a serious inquiry into the implications of Bill C-116 for the Canadian publishing industry, with a resultant recommendation that a return to the calculation of postal rates on the basis of circulation should take place.
At the core of this submission is the need for a fair, speedy and cheap postal system. I, for one, have never felt particularly discouraged about the fact that the Post Office did not return a profit. I am much more discouraged by the almost total breakdown in delivery of second-class and third-class mail, to say nothing about the fact that the delivery of even first-class mail seems to be disrupted all too often.
The government might also examine the speed and efficiency of second-class mail service, as subscription sales are surely dependent on people getting their magazines at the time they expect them. I suppose that other than on some of the more emotional social issues, the largest volume of mail members of parliament receive comes from frustrated constituents who are upset about the inadequacy of the postal service. If we are to judge by the quality of the first-class mail service in Canada, the publishing industry is indeed in deep trouble.
The last major point I wish to make-I hope the government will accept some of these submissions-has to do with the distribution system. If I might say so, the minister made a somewhat casual reference to this sector. But there is something he could do today, by fiat, if he wanted to: he could see to it that all the leases with respect to kiosks and magazine counters in Canadian airports, for example, contain a provision requiring adequate display and distribution of Canadian periodicals.
In this area, the minister need not worry about the constitutional aspect, though undoubtedly there are constitutional aspects attached to the establishment of a more thorough-going distribution system. He could give us earnest of his intention, however, if he were to apply such a provision immediately throughout establishments controlled by the Department of Transport, the Canadian National system, Crown corporations, and so on. In this very city of Ottawa there must be enough kiosks in government buildings to enable the minister to make an excellent start in providing a better distribution system. One of the things that has bothered me for many years is the overwhelming number of United States periodicals on display at Canadian airports. If one succeeds in finding a Canadian magazine among them, it shows one is a good explorer indeed.
Thirteen of the 14 magazine distribution firms operating in this country are American-owned. It follows that Canadian newsstands are inundated with American overflow copy to the extent that only 9 per cent of Canadian magazine sales are newsstand sales. Newsstands and other agencies distributing periodicals should be required to ensure the fair treatment and exposure of Canadian magazines. I do not have the statistics, but I would guess that most of the magazines making up the 9 per cent to which I
Non-Canadian Publications
have just referred are sold in the large cities. Those of us who represent constituencies in other than the large cities find it frustrating not to be able to locate Canadian periodicals on the newsstands.
Newsstands and other agencies distributing periodicals should be required to ensure that fair treatment and exposure of Canadian magazines takes place. The government might also consider instituting an establishment of national distribution to guarantee the promotion and circulation of periodicals. As an immediate measure, the government should encourage the display and sale of Canadian magazines at federal installations and Information Canada offices. Public corporations, as I said earlier-and there are several of them-are providing a selection of our own publications for their clientele.
I mentioned earlier that another need in respect of a positive policy for Canadian periodicals is cash flow- money; capital. Consideration should be given to the establishment of a national periodicals development corporation or, if the government resists this-and I would be surprised, because this is a government with a proliferation of agencies, boards and commissions-there could be a modification or an expansion of one or other of the existing structures, for example the Canada Council, for the purpose of granting both resources of capital and assistance to the publishing industry.
If I can interpolate one small comment, I think the Canada Council system, now, of distributing books to some of the smaller libraries of Canada, is a worth-while program and one that could well be copied for Canadian periodicals, providing subscriptions to the smaller and less adequately funded libraries in our country. I might say that in my own constituency, this very year two packages of Canadian books were sent out to what might be called libraries of modest size and it was a matter of great personal satisfaction that this occurred. I have always felt it would be very helpful if the same policy were adopted with regard to some of our periodicals.
In co-operation with the provinces, such an agency might make grants available to journalists engaged in the periodicals industry to further develop and assist the talents and energies of Canadian writers. As an immediate measure, the council should expand its present book purchase program to include Canadian magazine subscriptions for public and school libraries. The government might also consider the purchase of a more substantial amount of advertising space. I think the minister alluded to this matter. I may say that the Saturday Night people, when they saw us last week, alluded to advertising space in Canadian periodicals rather strongly to counteract the possible loss in advertising revenues resulting from the present legislation.
My only caveat in respect of government advertising is that it is one of the great, unexamined pork barrels, as I understand it, in the government system. A government that prides itself on being Mister Clean seems to dibble and dabble in advertising patronage to an extravagant extent.
My theme, and I hope the minister will agree, has been one of trying to suggest to parliament ways in which the

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
periodicals industry in this country could be made much more healthy by a distribution system, an improvement in second-class mail, in cash flow, and so on. I resist very much, intellectually and in every other way, the matter of Canadian content which was so casually alluded to by the minister in his speech. I resist having officials, by some inadequately explained measure, trying to add up what is or is not content. As a matter of fact, in the minister's speech he said it might be possible for all the stories in a magazine to be written by offshore people, with no article alluding to this country, yet the magazine could get a Canadian content rating. This paradox is the very issue, and particularly when we get into the matter of news we are getting into an area that through the years-

speechtext: Or opinion.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: News or opinion, as my leader has said. Then we are getting into an area that through the years has given tyrannical governments the power that free men have resisted through the ages. That, then, is the tenor of this speech. I have tried to make it positive rather than negative, and I adopt as the party position the suggestion that positive rather than negative policies will substantially increase the availability, the health and the viability of the periodicals industry in this country.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the NDP welcomes, as long overdue, this legislation to end the special status for advertising in Time and Reader's Digest.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
I hear a bit of applause from the Liberal side. Maybe they should wait a few minutes. While the legislation is welcomed, I regret that this government and its predecessors have dillied and dallied so long that the Canadian periodicals industry is in the sad state it is in today. Had the government acted on the royal commission report back in the early 1960s, or even on the special Senate committee report of the early 1970s perhaps the situation would not be as desperate as it is.
All members of the House must, or should realize the importance of magazines in Canada. If we are concerned about Canadian independence and identity, we must be concerned about the health of the Canadian magazine industry. We have heard much concern expressed in debates in the House about the economic independence of Canada, and we now have on the books the foreign investments review act, which is a token gesture because it is not totally proclaimed yet, in an effort to regain control of our economy which in so many sectors is foreign owned; 60 per cent, for example, in manufacturing and 90 per cent in terms of oil resources. We seem concerned about Canadian independence and identity in the broadcasting field, in that the Canadian Radio-Television Commission has suggested 80 per cent Canadian control of the broadcasting media, cablevision and Canadian stations and has also advocated 60 per cent Canadian content in programming.
I maintain that our cultural independence and identity is just as essential as our economic independence if we are to remain a sovereign nation and a sovereign people. What is the good of achieving economic sovereignty if we lose
our identity in the process? What good is there in Canadi-anizing industry if we ourselves are Americanized through what we read?
Therefore, I suggest that magazines are special and have a vital and important role to play in promoting the Canadian identity. I would maintain that magazines are as important as our national railway was at the time of confederation, in terms of binding the nation together and helping Canadians understand one another from coast to coast.
Magazines are the only national press we have. They are the only media whereby we can have an in-depth study of Canada and Canadians. Magazines are not bound by daily deadlines or the pressures that newspapers, television and radio have to meet in order to get their message out on time. In respect of magazines, time is provided for more analysis which is sadly lacking in the news media in this country.
Through magazines, we as Canadians can become aware of the needs, problems, successes and failures of Canadians living in Newfoundland, British Columbia, the Northwest Territories and all points in between. That need, to me, is very essential today because our cultural identity is being eroded by the presence of a huge country and a huge entertainment industry south of our border. We often know more about American history and politics than our own, through the medium of television. Often our heroes are Hollywood stars and others to whom we are introduced through the medium of the American movies which Canadians watch.
Many of our entertainment figures or people in the music industry are Americans, because of the penetration of American music. Also, in the news media we are subject to a heavy dependence of foreign correspondents to interpret the news of the world, not only in terms of reporting but in terms of news and film clips from CBS and other United States networks. Because we do not have too many Canadian foreign correspondents, we rely heavily on Associated Press, United Press International, and Reuters.
Through this process, Canadians get a view of the world through the eyes of other people. Indeed, it seems that our very lifestyle is more and more becoming Americanized. When I was up in the Yukon Territory I was amazed to see, in Whitehorse, a Colonel Sanders Kentucky Fried Chicken outlet; One cannot go anywhere in Canada without seeing McDonald's hamburger stands in the cities, American-produced cars, and so on. Our whole lifestyle seems to be more and more influenced by the American presence.
Our magazine industry is no exception. Magazines in Canada generally are dominated by foreign publications. For example, Playboy magazine collects about as much money in Canada as the 17 largest English-language magazines combined. We have competition from United States news magazines which have access to resources with which Canadian news magazines cannot compete. Therefore, I say it is very important that we have a healthy and expanding Canadian magazine industry because magazines have a vital role to play in countering the cultural influence the United States is having on our citizens. We

May 8, 1975

need Canadian magazines to interpret Canadianism to Canadians and to interpret the world to Canada.
As I said earlier, our magazine industry is in deep trouble; it is facing severe and unfair competition from foreign magazines. This industry-I want to underline this-is in trouble because of the procrastination, lack of concern and shortsightedness of Liberal and Conservative governments over the past 15 years. Very briefly, I should like to document that statement. I would say, for example, that as early as 1922 the Magazine Publishers Association of Canada asked for protective tariffs on foreign periodicals. The Conservative government of 1931 did levy such a tax, but the Liberal government in 1936 removed it. The result was that foreign magazines began to penetrate into Canada and the two most important foreign magazines, namely, Time and Reader's Digest, in the late 1940s and early 1950s began to capture a great deal of the advertising revenue in Canada. In fact, by 1955 those two magazines, Times and Reader's Digest, had captured one-third of the magazine advertising revenue in Canada.
In the same year, only one-fifth of all consumer magazines read in Canada were Canadian. In light of this trend of foreign domination of the magazine industry, in 1957 the Liberal government finally imposed a 20 per cent tax on advertising in Canadian editions of foreign periodicals. However, with a change in government when the Conservatives came in a year later in 1958, that legislation was repealed because of the very heavy pressure by the United States government. I think one should ask oneself why the United States government was so concerned about the status of Time and Reader's Digest in this country.
I should like to elaborate the thesis that the United States government is concerned about these two magazines, because they really are agents of United States diplomacy. In 1960 and 1961, finally, the Conservative government instituted the Royal Commission on Publications which recommended that an end be put to the right of advertisers in foreign magazines in Canada to deduct the cost of advertising for income tax purposes. It was typical of Conservative procrastination that the government refused to accept the recommendation and exempted Time Magazine and Reader's Digest. Certain political events took place, the government was defeated and no subsequent legislation was introduced. Then when the Liberals returned to power in 1965 we find that once more the United States government put very strong pressure on the Canadian government to officially, through legislation exempt Time magazine and Reader's Digest from any future legislation to end the tax advantage for advertisers in those two foreign magazines.
The minister of finance at that time, Mr. Walter Gordon, said that the government came under such pressure that the United States was threatening not to agree to the Canada-US auto pact and was threatening to reduce Canadian oil exports to the United States if these two magazines were not exempted from the foreign periodicals tax legislation. As a typical example of the Liberals bowing to the United States on this important issue, the two magazines were officially exempted. Then in 1969 the government instituted the special Senate Committee on the Mass Media which reiterated the problems of the publishing industry in this country and reached the same
Non-Canadian Publications
conclusion that had been reached by the previous royal commission. I should like to quote from the Senate committee's report:
It seems plain to us that if Time and Digest are allowed to maintain their present competitive advantage, it will become increasingly difficult for existing magazines to survive, and for new ones to be launched ... but we are satisfied that the long-term prospects for Canadian periodical industry-and probably the short-term as well- would be enhanced by removal of subsidized foreign competition.
There we have evidence through the years of the publishing industry expressing its concern, of a royal commission after exhaustive study coming out with concrete recommendations, of a Senate committee also coming out with concrete recommendations, but this government and its predecessor having refused to act until now. What happened to the Canadian magazine industry in the interim when those Liberal and Conservative governments delayed? It is interesting to look through the records and see what went on.
In the 1920s there were 96 consumer magazines in existence, and during that period 23 of them folded and died. In the 1930s, 75 magazines were started but 65 of them folded. In the 1940s, 92 magazines were started and 70 died. In the 1950s, 29 new magazines were started and a total of 50 died. By the 1960s we had 250 new magazines and 137 died. Meanwhile, especially in the 1950s and 1960s, Time and Reader's Digest were leaping forward because of their special status regarding advertisers in their magazines. The circulation of Time rose from 215,000 in 1960 to 557,000 today, and the circulation of Reader's Digest rose from 1 million in 1960 to 1.2 million today. But perhaps even more important than that, Time and Reader's Digest together have now captured 48 per cent of all magazine advertising revenue in Canada, that is to say, over $17 million.
Time and Reader's Digest, two foreign magazines with Canadian editions, unlike any other foreign magazine such as Newsweek, U.S. News and World Report, have a special status so far as advertisers are concerned. They are treated as Canadian magazines for advertising, income tax purposes. Therefore, Time and Reader's Digest have an unfair advantage over any other foreign magazine circulating in Canada. Time and Reader's Digest also have the advantage of being subsidiaries of foreign publications, which prevents Canadian magazines being on an equal, competitive footing with them.
That is something on which I would like to elaborate in my speech. Neither Time nor Reader's Digest can claim to be Canadian magazines with regard to ownership, content or editorial control. The principle of fairness and equity must dictate that they be treated under the law as foreign publications, which they are. This has been the policy advocated by the NDP for years. Bill C-58 which is before us defines Time and Reader's Digest as foreign magazines for income tax purposes. It will end the special advantages they have received under section 19 of the Income Tax Act, and its aim is to free more advertising revenue for Canadian magazines by diverting such revenue away from Time and Reader's Digest.
What do we mean by a Canadian magazine? The minister gave a rather vague definition with regard to content. Earlier, other ministers spoke about a 75 per cent content

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
which had to be Canadian, but the minister said simply that the content of a Canadian magazine had to be substantially different from any non-Canadian publication. The other aspect of a Canadian magazine must be that effective editorial control is exercised in Canada, and that at least 75 per cent ownership of the magazine must be Canadian.
How do Time and Reader's Digest measure up to those criteria? For example, in no way can Time be considered a Canadian magazine. It has a mere five pages of Canadian news, which represents about 10 per cent of its content. Its editorial control resides in the United States in its parent company, and Time Canada is wholly owned by Time Incorporated of the U.S.
Reader's Digest has been making a pitch; it has been lobbying members of parliament, getting the public to write letters and trying to argue that it should have a special status, it deserves a special deal because, somehow, it is more Canadian than Time. Reader's Digest only has 24 per cent Candian content in its English edition and only 12 per cent Canadian content in its French edition. Its editorial control resides in the United States-every article published in Reader's Digest has to meet the approval of the editorial board in the U.S.-and only 32 per cent of the shares of Reader's Digest are open to Canadians for purchasing. But we should remember that not all of those shares are owned by Canadians. As the president of the company, Mr. Zimmerman, said, some of the shares have filtered back to the United States.
But even if Time or Reader's Digest were to go public and issue shares in Canada, even if they had something like 75 per cent Canadian ownership, that, to me, would be fudging the issue, because when we talk about magazines and news the key issue is not who owns the actual publication, but who controls the editorial policy and, hence, the content of that magazine. Unless that kind of control resides in the hands of Canadians, those magazines will still be promoting and interpreting Canada and the world from a foreign viewpoint. We cannot get around the fact that Time and Reader's Digest have been, and will continue to interpret America and the world through American eyes and from an American viewpoint.
I could give many examples but I think two would suffice. Can anyone in the House recall, during that sad conflict of the Viet Nam war and American involvement over a decade, any substantial criticism in either Time magazine or Reader's Digest of American policy in Viet Nam? It was only when the tide turned in the U.S. and America wanted to get out of Viet Nam because of the realization of the morass in which they found themselves, that we found these two magazines publishing critical analyses of that war. But earlier on, when other magazines in Canada and the world were publishing critical articles-and I say "critical" in a positive sense; you can have both sides of the story in the same publication-that was not true of Time and Reader's Digest.
More recently, when Canada wanted to sell locomotives to the United States through the M. L. Worthington firm, the U.S. government tried to prohibit that subsidiary from doing so, using the Trading with the Enemy Act. If you looked up that issue of Time magazine you would notice that Time was being apologetic, trying to justify the U.S.

government's imposition of the Trading with the Enemy Act. What I am saying is that basically we are not getting news from the Canadian perspective in those five pages of Time or the articles selected for Reader's Digest.
What other advantages do these two magazines have other than their special status with regard to income tax? It seems to me that they have an unfair competitive advantage for a number of reasons. First of all, they have a great economic advantage over their Canadian competitors because their editorial content is supplied by their parent company in the United States. This means that the two magazines can obtain material that is costly in terms of research, and so on, at a cut rate, at subsidized cost, from its parent company. No Canadian magazine can do that.
Another advantage is that these magazines have a tax advantage over their American competitors selling in Canada, because only these two magazines are permitted to have their advertisers deduct the cost of advertising for Canadian income tax purposes. Another great advantage these two magazines have is that they have captured almost all of the magazine advertising revenue in Canada. Therefore, on the principle of equitable treatment it would seem that we have to end the special status of Time and Reader's Digest. They should be treated on the same basis as any other foreign magazine and should not have any special privileges for advertisers.
Why else should we end the special status? It seems that by not having an advantage regarding income tax, Time and Reader's Digest advertisers will begin to divert advertising revenue to Canadian magazines and other Canadian media. I do not have any illusions that all the revenue freed from advertising in Time and Reader's Digest will go to magazines, but it may go to Canadian television and radio. At least we will be able to keep this revenue in Canada, rather than seeing the bulk of the revenue raised by advertising in Canada flow back to the parent companies in the United States. Time and Reader's Disgest have carried out a survey showing that only 19 per cent of the freed revenue would go to Canadian magazines. This would be something over $3 million. We do not know whether that survey is accurate; but even if it is, $3 million would be beneficial as cash flow for Canadian magazines.
It seems, also, that we must stop the advertising advantages of Time and Reader's Digest because of what they are doing to regional editions. Time especially has 12 regional editions; it can attract local and regional advertisers, through special rates, to advertise in the magazine for those local and regional audiences. That, therefore, inhibits local and regional magazines such as Toronto Life and Vancouver Life. Once we end the special advertising advantages for Time and Reader's Digest in their regional editions, we will help promote regional magazines which are a vital part of the Canadian industry.
It seems that the revenue raised through ending this tax advantage will be a great boon to existing Canadian magazines and it will encourage others to get into the market and expand. I would like to point out that this bill will not necessarily mean that the Canadian editions of Time and
May 8, 1975

Reader's Digest will fold; they still have a large circulation, which must be attractive to some advertisers. We should remember that the revenue of Reader's Digest does not primarily come from advertising in Canada. Three-quarters of the revenue of Reader's Digest comes from sources other than advertising revenue, that is, from book clubs and record clubs. Even if the Canadian editions of Time and Reader's Digest were to cease, Canadians would still be able to buy the American editions just as they can now buy Newsweek, Playboy or any other American magazine.
If the two magazines were to fold-and I do not think it is inevitable that they would-their staff could certainly be absorbed by the Canadian publishing industry. It seems to me that ending their special status will stimulate the Canadian weekly news magazine industry. Already, Macleans has indicated it will move to that kind of format. There are other publishers expressing similar intentions. In conclusion, I say that we have an important need for a strong and healthy Canadian periodicals industry. I would like to read from the report of the royal commission of 1960:
Only a truly Canadian printing press, one with the feel of Canada and directly responsible to Canada, can give us the critical analysis, the informed discourse and dialogue which are indispensable in a sovereign society.
Neither Time nor Reader's Digest conform to that concept of Canadian publishing. Nor, by definition of their content and editorial policy, can they ever hope to conform to that definition. I again quote from the royal commission:
A nation's domestic advertising expenditure should be devoted to the support of its own media of communications, and ... a genuinely Canadian periodical press can only exist if it has access to a fair share of domestic advertising.
For years the Liberal government has let Time and Reader's Digest capture half of that revenue through the special status given to advertisers in those magazines. Now, hopefully, this trend will be reversed. But this bill is not the be-all and end-all. We need more positive measures. We need a comprehensive periodicals policy. We need to end foreign domination of ownership of magazine distributing agencies in this country. We need to revise postal rates for magazines to end discrimination, especially against our smaller magazines. We need to take measures to discourage the overflow circulation of foreign magazines. For example, in 1961 it amounted to over $150 million per year, compared to a domestic production of only $40 million.
We should consider the example of Switzerland, which imposes a postal surcharge on foreign periodicals. Germany imposes a tax on foreign periodicals. We could use the revenues thus raised to promote a Canadian magazine industry. So far, this government has failed to move positively in those directions. We still do not have a policy for periodicals.
I would like to reiterate my faith in Canadian writers and publishers. When the CRTC demanded higher Canadian content in music, we saw how this caused our recording industry to flourish. I believe the same kind of talent exists in Canadian writers and publishers. A few Canadian magazines in Canada have achieved high audience penetration. This bill will end the unfair advantage of Time and Reader's Digest and create more equitable competitive conditions in this country for the magazine indus-
Non-Canadian Publications
try. The audience is there; so is the talent. To argue that the Canadian magazine industry cannot now grow and flourish is negative and defeatist.
The NDP welcomes Bill C-58, Mr. Speaker. Had the government accepted the royal commission recommendations in the early sixties, the industry would not be in the precarious state in which it finds itself. This bill is not a panacea, but it is an important step in the right direction and we welcome it as long overdue.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I ought to congratulate the Chair. We are happy to see a former Deputy Speaker in the Chair again.
I am somewhat suprised by the presentation of Bill C-58 which aims to remove the provisions allowing deduction of expenses for Canadians who buy advertising space in Time and Reader's Digest magazines, under the pretext that this will enable them to have magazines of equal quality in Canada.
I listened carefully to the minister's speech this afternoon. I have tried to find an argument that would convince me that the passage of Bill C-58 will enable Canadian magazines to improve their publication in such a way as to be appreciated in the same manner as Reader's Digest by the Canadian people, and particularly by the French-Canadians. The numerous letters I received on this subject endorse my view. In none of all the letters I received asked the Member of Parliament to support this bill. On the contrary, they asked that the legislation enacted by Parliament with regard to periodicals listed in the 1965 act be maintained and fully enforced.
Mr. Speaker, in the 1965 act, amended in 1971, Canadian publications are defined in such a way as to exempt Time and Reader's Digest from the legislation. As a matter of fact, it was considered at that time that Canadian publications are those which are 75 to 100 per cent Canadian owned. However, there was an exception for periodicals edited in whole or in part in Canada in 1965, and such was the situation of the two magazines involved.
I am of the opinion that the government should first of all fully apply to Time and Reader's Digest the definition given in the Income Tax Act concerning the exact nature of a Canadian periodical. It is stated in the act that such a publication must be at least 75 per cent Canadian-owned by Canadians having a right of undisturbed possession on the shares in their name.
It is also provided in the legislation that in order to be recognized as a Canadian edition, a publication has to be drafted, edited and printed in Canada.
Then, Time and Reader's Digest are already complying with these legal requirements. Well, I should like also to indicate what financial benefits these two publications are bringing to the development of the Canadian economy. First of all, their combined annual turnover amounts to $30 million, which is quite impressive, and they do spend 90 cents out of every dollar here in Canada. They have $8 million in capital investment in Canada, that is in land, buildings, machinery and equipment of all sorts. There are
5604

May 8, 1975

The Royal Assent
also 500 people earning a living in Canada as their employees.
There are also 1,000 other jobs, maybe more, which exist only because these firms are using Canadian materials. These firms could very well have done without having to use more and more Canadian products, but they have decided to take into account the fact that they are operating in Canada, that they have the chance of being published in Canada and so they seek to increase their business dealings with Canadian suppliers.
Moreover, it has not been said five out of the six members on the board of directors who administer the Reader's Digest operations in Canada are well-known Canadian personalities.
Also, as far as the Canadian culture is concerned, the selecting, reviewing and writing of the entire contents of every copy is all done in Canada, both in French and in English. The English contribution is of course larger than the French, but it remains that the bilingual character of our country is respected. According to my information, there are also some 80 writers, artists and lay-out men employed in putting the periodicals together. Moreover, there are 80 writers who are making a selection of articles out of other publications to make it a truly informative and objective periodical and to encourage Canadians to read these articles.
These periodicals also contribute Canadian articles in foreign editions of the Reader's Digest throughout the world, which represent a potential readership of 105 million people. I think that this is an excellent vehicle for promoting Canada abroad. These are things we must consider and keep in mind. I see, Mr. Speaker, that you are about to interrupt me. May I call it five o'clock?
