AIR CANADA CONTRACT, ADDITIONS, REVISIONS AND AMENDMENTS THERETO
speechtext:
That an order of the House do issue for a copy of the Air Canada contract and all additions, revisions and amendments thereto.
He said: Mr. Speaker, the government's refusal to provide the information requested by motion No. 24 in my name is a classic example of this government's perpetual desire to function under a veil of secrecy, no matter what the consequences may be, and without regard to the public's right to know and the public interest. Because of your earlier announcement, Mr. Speaker, I regret that my motion will not be debated for as long as I wish. I say, in all sincerity, that I find the government's reasoning incredible, its refusal to release information requested by motion No. 24 unbelievable, and if the scene we are witnessing were to be acted out in the National Arts Centre we should find it humorous. Unfortunately, this scene is taking place in the House of Commons and it is beyond a joke; it is downright contemptible.
On a previous occasion, the parliamentary secretary said that the Air Canada contract alluded to contain considerable confidential information relating to the organization, operation and maintenance of Air Canada lines. I ask the parliamentary secretary, or whoever is to respond, to tell us what this confidential information is. What is so confidential about it that it cannot be formally released to this House, especially as the contract I have requested is readily available from the Public Archives of Canada. I have the document here and I will be prepared to table it if the

May 8, 1975

government or the spokesman on the other side of the House is not prepared to do so.
When I raised this matter previously, the parliamentary secretary went on to say that Air Canada competitors are not obliged to provide such information or expose their contractual arrangements to similar scrutiny. He then said that to place Air Canada in such a disadvantageous position would not be in the public interest. That is utter nonsense. Air Canada is in a special position and enjoys advantages which other airlines do not enjoy. Under the provisions of section 16(7) of the Aeronautics Act, and sections 14 and 23 of the Air Canada Act, the governor in council directs the CTC to grant Air Canada permission to serve points X, Y or Z. The airline does not need to go through the regular channels, the ordeal of petitions, hearings and red tape to obtain the routes they choose. Air Canada is given preferential treatment and quite a free hand with regard to route approvals, as well as a free hand in schedules, levels and frequency of services provided thereafter. Section 5 of the Air Canada contract of 1950 reads:
The schedules, frequencies and non-stop operations on the air services herein or hereinafter designated and the service to points of call herein or hereinafter authorized shall be determined by the corporation in accordance with traffic and operational requirements, technical facilities and government regulations.
It could be argued that Air Canada tends to abuse its special privileges. For example, consider how the Sud-bury-Thunder Bay route was awarded. It is unlikely, if Air Canada refuses to provide the service it is supposed to provide until prodded by another airline, that the other airline will go through the expensive procedure of applying for the route if that route is to be ultimately taken over by Air Canada. For the parliamentary secretary to suggest that it is improper to expose the terms and conditions of Air Canada contracts is totally absurd, given that Air Canada is in a preferred position, that it functions as a quasi-monopoly and that it is owned by Canadians, for the benefit of Canadians. The airline's purpose, after all, is to provide for the speedy and efficient transportation of passengers and goods across Canada and points outside. Over and above that, the corporation must be answerable to parliament and thereby to the people of Canada.
That brings me to another point I want to make about all Crown corporations. I am referring to the whole question of disclosure relating to Crown corporations or, rather, to the absence or lack of disclosure in the interests of the public. I also draw attention to the current practice in which we engage, to do with the examination and scrutiny by committees of parliament of the operations, affairs and activities of our Crown corporations. In my view, there are far too many restrictions relating to the important and basic issue of the examination of Crown corporations, as the motion we are debating now makes evident.
Let me give some more examples of what I mean. I draw the attention of the House to motion No. 77, which I brought forward in the previous parliament, as recorded on page 5507 of Hansard for July 11, 1973. That was a request for documents and had to do with some questionable dealings concerning a change in auditors. That was a fiasco. As well, I refer the House to the request for correspondence between Sunset Crest Ltd. and Air Canada.
Air Canada
This matter is the subject of a judicial inquiry. It seems to me that the government ought to have released such information and documents as were requested concerning Air Canada. If the affairs of Air Canada could have been scrutinized diligently and thoroughly by the transport committee, the story might now be different. The committee should have the power to look into the questionable actions indulged in by some people involved with Air Canada. But we were denied information about leases, arrangements, salaries, benefits, and so on.
Under our committee system it is almost impossible to examine and scrutinize effectively the activities of our Crown corporations. Although the officials of Crown corporations in theory answer to parliament, in fact they answer to no one except the government of the day. The result is evident. Air Canada is now being subjected to a judicial inquiry. Because of its insistence of secrecy aided and abetted by the government, the national airline finds itself in a period of turbulence and trouble. I submit, again, that if there were a requirement for disclosure, if officials of the company were forced to appear before a proper investigatory committee on a regular basis and testify, if they were forced to defend their actions and answer for them, the result would be good for the airline and would engender public confidence. As it is, the affairs of Air Canada are being probed by a judicial inquiry.
On the basis of what happened the last time these people appeared before a parliamentary committee we became convinced that, given the constraints of the present committee system under the rules, and because of present procedures and terms of reference, it would be impossible to get to the bottom of what causes the malaise within this company. That malaise has grown deeper because there has not been an effective check by parliament.
I think it is time we took a leaf from British parliamentary practice. That parliament has seen fit to establish a select committee which deals with specific nationalized industries. When it meets it looks into all aspects of the operation of a nationalized corporation, and looks in depth.
This practice, if adopted here, would do two things. It would provide for greater public disclosure; also, it would serve as an effective check on the behaviour of those charged with the responsibility and administration of that particular corporation. Considering the increased proliferation of Crown corporations in this country and the obvious need for greater parliamentary control, examination, and scrutiny, I recommend that this parliament should seriously consider the establishment of such a select committee. It should be a committee composed of members of parliament, with wide powers. It should be able to engage highly expert assistants. It should consider the operation of a Crown corporation not in a retrospective way but in a prospective way.
In the United Kingdom they have a committee which requires government agency officials to provide evidence requested by it. It is up to the committee to decide whether such information should be made public or not. This system imposes more effective parliamentary control over institutions of government and provides a needed system

of checks and balances. Our present committee system is too politically motivated. It functions in far too superficial a manner. The objectives of a special select committee on Crown corporations would be to review their operations experly, in a reasonable and constructive way and in the interests of the public and the welfare of the corporation.
It always appears somewhat ironic that the socialists continue to recommend nationalization. They say in that way the public will know what is going on, parliament will examine, parliament will be the final judge and the board will have to answer to parliament. That is sheer nonsense. In reality, the public has probably less access to the officers of socialized enterprises than the shareholders of capitalistic enterprises have to their officers. The more dogmatic the socialist theory becomes, the less access the people have to the operation of the socialist enterprise. If we are to have socialized enterprises established for the benefit of the people, then clearly they should be operated for the people and not for the government of the day.

Mr. Speaker, I do not intend to take very much time in this discussion since the parliamentary secretary has swallowed his earlier words and is now prepared to table documents which he previously withheld. Because I think it is a remarkable development, I want to deal with the demonstration that is inherent in the action by the parliamentary secretary today and the absolutely arbitrary method in which documents are considered to be confidential or not confidential.
We have a situation here where an Air Canada contract was regarded as confidential yesterday. Suddenly, today, by some act of magic or some magic wand, it is deemed to be acceptable to table it in the House of Commons. Yesterday it was confidential, today we can have it. That indicates how completely arbitrary the position of this government is as to keeping public information out of the public domain. There is obviously no consistent policy on the part of this government regarding information. There is no consistent policy with regard to what is to be held back in the public interest and what is to be made available to the House of Commons in the public interest.
We have known for some time that the government has no information policy except as indicated to me by an assistant deputy minister in a senior department, that is, to stamp "Confidential" on the toilet paper or any other paper which happens to be in circulation in the offices. Surely today we have underlined the complete absence of any kind of over-all policy regarding the public right to information. It has been made absolutely clear that the decision whether a document should be published or should remain secret is an arbitrary one depending on such things as the state of the moon, or which side of the bed the minister or the parliamentary secretary got out of in the morning.
Yesterday the document was so confidential that neither parliament nor the public could be permitted to see it. Today, by some magic occurrence, it can be tabled in the House of Commons. I welcome the tabling of the document. I welcome the latter-day conversion of the parliamentary secretary. I hope he does not disappear from our midst as a result of his conversion to the point of view that parliament has a right to obtain information with which it is properly concerned.
While the decision is very welcome, it demonstrates, as nothing else can, how arbitrary is the information policy followed by the government and the complete lack of consistency regarding what will be kept secret and what will be made public. It also underlines the futility of the guidelines applied to the release of information. We now know that the only guideline is what members on the treasury benches opposite want to do. In a system which is supposed to be concerned about the informed participation of the citizenry, that is obviously not a proper viewpoint to take.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is in a very unpleasant mood that this House is dealing with a bill which, offhand, may seem of little importance but which is nevertheless very important. I wish to continue the remarks I had begun before the private members' hour.
I must say that this is the third time that this matter has been put before the House and twice the Liberal government contended that to allow the tax deductibility of advertising expenses of both magazines was beneficial for the Canadian people. How is it that it was justifiable in 1965 and in 1971 and that it should be condemnable in 1975? Was the government right in 1965 and in 1971 or is he right in 1975? Such are the questions which must be asked and about which Parliament is entitled to answers from the government. What justifies the government's new attitude on this matter which is raised today the same way it was ten years ago?
It might be interesting, Mr. Speaker, to review the reasons put forward by the government members at that time and those put forward in 1975. Why this policy reversal? As for me, as member for Bellechasse, I am wondering about that. I would like very much to get answers and very clear explanations. Why the change in attitude? Will that be really beneficial for the Canadian people? Will the Americans be the losers? In short, what will be changed? I think we are entitled to very clear answers from the minister who piloted this bill. As for me, I am ready to receive the explanations that will be provided so that we may give valid answers to our electors, since we have received many inquiries on that matter.
I imagine all hon. members are in the same situation. Many people have taken the trouble to write asking that we take such or such a stand. The majority of letters I received, as I said this afternoon, were mostly in favour of maintaining the status quo.
So can the minister tell the House whether those who advertise or those who own the magazines in question will be the losers? Who will be the losers? Who will be the winners? We need to know. In view of the large public appeal of Reader's Digest I tend to think that Canadians will continue to advertise in those magazines, even without the benefits available under the act. I am giving a pretty neutral opinion but I think that actually, with or without the benefits, in view of the large circulation of those magazines, current advertisers will continue to advertise. So, working on that assumption, I consider that Canadians will be the losers from a monetary standpoint. According to a Canadian Fact poll, even if Reader's Digest loses advertisers, that does not necessarily mean that other Canadian magazines will benefit because they do not have the same circulation; proper consideration must be given to how many people will be reached by an ad.
The same poll shows that 85 per cent of surveyed advertisers want Section 19 of the Income Tax Act to remain as it is. According to the surveys made by Canadian Fact of Digest subscribers who were asked whether they found the magazine to be a threat to our Canadian culture, 65 per cent answered no. So, to have a valid opinion, the reader must be consulted in order to find out whether subscribers
feel robbed of their culture by reading such or such an article in that magazine. Twenty-two per cent do not have an opinion or did not want to answer; 7 per cent agree to some extent that it may affect the Canadian culture, and 6 per cent fully agree and are convinced that it is likely to hurt the Canadian culture.
So one can conclude that there is a ratio of 6 per cent to 65 per cent on the cultural side. I would not want to leave the impression that I am more in favour of Americans than Canadians. There is no need to try and show that my preference certainly goes to Canadians and my country. I must analyse the situation objectively in order to be able to make a decision. I hope it will be the right one and if I happen to be wrong, I would not do any worse than those who made mistakes in 1965 and 1971.
However, if the present legislation could be enforced more strictly, I think that eventually the Canadian Reader's Digest would be owned entirely by Canadians. We would then benefit from the experience and the great value of a first rate magazine. I am not attempting to depreciate the others, but I must say that we tried to develop in Canada magazines of true merit. I recognize that we have succeeded, but it does not mean that we should no longer appreciate the fact that many Canadian readers subscribe to a magazine that reports a great number of facts, discoveries and data from other countries that could benefit Canadians.
All the same, we must be sincere and fair in our legislation. I think that each of us is striving to be in the reasons that we put forward to justify our decisions.
I for one remember that a few years ago in the province of Quebec the alarm was sounded with this slogan: Masters in our own house. I remember quite well. Thank God,
I still have some memory. Newspaper pages were not big enough to print the key of the masters in their own house, it had to be printed diagonally. Quebecers believed in that memorable phrase: Masters in our own house. However, ten years later we realize that we are not any more masters in our own house than we were before.
One after the other, the Quebec governements have kept going to New York to beg for the money needed to develop our natural resources. Then, we are not yet masters in our own house, we still depend on American financiers. If my memory serves me well, the Canadian government and all the provinces, including Manitoba, did the same thing. They are still going to the United States to ask permission to develop our natural resources. The credit of our country is based on the work of Canadians that is guaranteed by our natural resources, the processing of all kinds of products that our people can use to satisfy their needs. In 1975, we still have to ask permission to New York financiers when we could do otherwise.
We depend on American finance when our country, under the authority of Parliament, the House in which we are sitting tonight, the "salon de la race", should be the supreme authority in our country. We could proceed otherwise under existing legislation, if we decided to act, to exercise fully the authority of a sovereign Parliament and I am in favour of a sovereign Parliament. I am so today, as I was yesterday and will be tomorrow. Because I believe Parliament is the chamber of the representatives of the whole country, of all parts of Canada. According to the

May 8, 1975

Constitution, we are sent here, in a democratically-organized chamber, in order to legislate, to pass laws, to administer the country, and we do hope that we will administer the country in a sovereign Parliament.
That is why I am convinced that we have authority to act legally and, then, to have the decisions of Parliament carried out by the government which consists in the Cabinet. Ministers are there for carrying out the decisions of Parliament. This is the way I feel our democracy should be.
If we do want our ministers to administer this country efficiently, we must give them tools, it is imperative that we show to the people of Canada that we are truly responsible at any level, even at the financial level which is as was said not so many years ago, the sinews of war. Well, if finance is the sinews of war, it is also the sinews of social peace which is a must to administer a country, to be able to really be an autonomous people, a people willing to be the master of its own destiny. I am convinced that the ministers here tonight in the House realize the full significance of what I am saying, and they perfectly know that I speak with the utmost sincerity, because I am fully aware that I am a member of this House which is the supreme authority in my country, and that I am ready to cooperate with all my colleagues, so that we could offer all organizations and citizens of this country with a healthy administration.
It is not only through writings, Mr. Speaker, that culture may be threatened or improved. What is going on with films and television? Nobody can stop Canadians with a TV set from turning it on and picking up American programs. Those programs come to us, our young people watch them. I have children at home and they look at those programs. They are interested or they are not. Future will tell us to what extent they may have been impressed, to what extent our culture will have been improved or destroyed by movies coming from the United States via television.
We let ourselves be overrun, although we do have people with real talent. It is always a surprise for me, week after week, whenever I have a chance to attend events put up by teachers or welfare organizations, who have young people acting in plays as we used to say. I am always favourably impressed with the easiness and talent displayed by our young boys and girls performing in sketches from which a moral can be drawn. They may not always understand the true meaning, of what they play but later on in life they will.
I remember when I was a small boy, I acted with seven girls in a play at the village school. I was the only boy at the end of the row, and I had a role to play. At the time I did not understand it very well, but today I do, and this is why I have a better understanding of Parliament's role.
I remember very well the last sentences which ended the play. We called it the grumbler's scene. There was this teacher who was always dissatisfied with his pupils. If the door was open, he would say: Shut the door. If the door was shut, he would say: Open the door. In my role I had this to say to the teacher: "Finally, do you know exactly what you want? A door must be either shut or open. How

do you want it?" And that ended the play. Well, we have the same thing here. We wish to be either a sovereign Parliament, or a dependent Parliament. How do we wish it to be? If we would have a sovereign Parliament, we will have to do what is needed. As far as I am concerned, I am aiming at the essentials, not what is accessory. The essentials I put above everything else. This is why I am against this legislation, because in my view it is not truly essential.
Other measures are vitally needed, but nothing is done about them. We did propose such measures. We are sometimes told that we, in the Social Credit Party, have it easy, because all we have to do is criticize, we have no responsibility as far as governing is concerned. I am well aware of that, but give us a chance to manage this country.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is not easy to rise tonight to speak on Bill C-58 and voice the criticisms which I intend to make this evening without being labelled anti-Canadian. I find it hard because I am as fiercely patriotic and as proud as anyone in the country. I long for the day when we, as Canadians, exercise control over many areas of our economy which are presently foreign dominated, but it is important that one remain realistic, and start from conditions as they exist and not from a position that we wish existed. On the one hand we must learn by our mistakes and not lack the courage to initiate measures which will correct those errors. On the other hand, we must face the consequences of our actions and not let our emotions control our minds.
What is this bill attempting to do? The Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner) has authorized his special assistant, when replying to letters, to state as follows:
In the government's view, it is necessary to remove from the Income Tax Act an inconsistency in the application of the law and a provision which works to the disadvantage of Canadian periodicals.
The letter goes on to say:
Whatever may be the results of the new legislation regarding the operations in Canada of Time and Reader's Digest, they will continue to be sold in Canada and provide the kind of reading material which is enjoyed by their many readers.
Who is being inconsistent? Has anyone told the Secretary of State that advertising revenues and the number of subscribers go hand in hand? When the readers of Reader's Digest are subscribing to American rather than Canadian editions will they, as proud Canadians, start buying Maclean's?
A press release issued by the Secretary of State quotes a royal commission as follows:
A nation's domestic advertising expenditure should be devoted to the support of its own media of communications, and ... a genuinely Canadian periodical press can only exist if it has access to a fair share of domestic advertising.
Let us look at that point for a moment, Mr. Speaker. In 1973 general magazines had a 2.4 per cent share of net
|Mr. Bechard.)
May 8, 1975

advertising revenues, or $32 million of a total of $1-1/3 billion. Radio took 11 per cent of that total and television 13 per cent. Radio and television have increased their share of the market, while the share to general magazines has decreased. The real competition for advertising revenues is not foreign controlled magazines but other media. Even amongst magazines, have the Canadian magazines fared badly in comparison to American controlled competition' Miss Chatelaine, Chatelaine and Maclean's have all experienced greater growth than Reader's Digest.
The three Maclean-Hunter publications had a total advertising revenue in 1973 of over $12 million, or 42 per cent of the total advertising revenue of the publications comprising the Magazine Association of Canada. This compares with $6 million for Reader's Digest. I do not believe I am being unfair in suggesting that the motivation of Peter Newman might be profit rather than patriotism. Of course it could be argued that the two go together.
A survey conducted by Canadian Facts Limited indicated that only 7 per cent of the advertising revenues of Reader's Digest would be diverted to Canadian magazines. That is approximately $400,000.
What is the real cost to Canada? Inspection of Reader's Digest Association (Canada) Limited records indicates that five of a board of six Digest directors are Canadian. All of the officers of the company are Canadian citizens, all 500 employees are permanent residents of Canada, and the company gives work indirectly to at least 1,000 other Canadians.
The two magazines are fully edited in Canada for Canadians.
Reader's Digest employs some 80 editors, graphic and production staff on books and magazines. Both magazines have substantial Canadian content amounting to an annual average of 24 per cent English and almost 15 per cent French. Almost 80 Canadian freelance writers, researchers and artists look to Reader's Digest books and magazines as a market for their work. The company has invested $8 million in buildings and manufacturing equipment. Reader's Digest Canadian produced magazines, books, record packages, and educational materials are welcomed as suitable for all age groups.
Close to six million Canadians read and enjoy the Canadian edition of the Digest every month. Reader's Digest Canadian material is made available to, and much of it is used by other editions around the world. Some articles receive exposure to 100 million readers in 13 languages. Reader's Digest has made some 32 per cent of its common stock available to Canadians through a public issue, the only Digest company in the world to do so. Shareholders bought their stock with the understanding that the company's operations were not under any threat at the time the stock was issued. Reader's Digest had that assurance from the government.
Reader's Digest has exceeded every guideline for corporate citizenship ever declared by a government of Canada. The Digest has already outlined to the Secretary of State the economic alternatives facing it if section 19(2) is removed. The only one that would leave it in even a marginally profitable position was based on the following
Non-Canadian Publications
assumptions: ceasing publication of the French language edition, which for years has been subsidized by other profitable operations; importing all English language editorial material from the U.S., with no Canadian editing and selection of articles; dismissing English and French editorial staffs and reducing employment elsewhere in the company. Survival on these terms would mean substantial loss of employment, reduced Digest expenditures in Canada, the loss of the French edition, and the abandonment of Canadian content-in other words a complete negation of Canadianization policies built up over the last 30 years.

speechtext:
French-Canadian readers, 1.3 million of them, stand to lose an edition in their own language edited by French-Canadians. French-language editions published in France or other francophone countries are not a practical alternative for French-Canadians.
English-Canadians would lose the substantial Canadian content now in the magazine-24 per cent last year, rising to 30 per cent. They would lose the research, complete editing and article selection now performed by the Canadian editorial team, and would receive instead a magazine edited and designed for American readers. Canadian authors would lose a good market for their work. Reader's Digest Canadian edition's articles about Canada could not be financially supported, and thus would no longer circulate world-wide to an audience of 100 million readers.
Canadian magazine growth since protective legislation was introduced in 1965 has been healthy. Eighty-seven new Canadian magazines, each with a circulation of over
10,000,	have emerged since 1965. Total annual circulation of these magazines is 199 million copies. Moreover, with some exceptions, established Canadian magazines have done well. Last August, Lloyd Hodgkinson, publisher of Maclean's, was quoted in the Toronto Globe and Mail as saying, "We have just had the three most prosperous years in the last ten at Maclean's, Chatelaine and Miss Chatelaine."
Has the present Canadian publishing industry considered what would be the effect on it if other countries adopted a requirement on ownership and content similar to that detailed by the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Basford)? Thomson Newspapers Limited, through U.S. subsidiaries, publishes some 49 daily and seven weekly newspapers in the United States. Maclean-Hunter Limited in the United Kingdom publishes business periodicals through a wholly-owned subsidiary. In the United States Maclean-Hunter Limited publishes business periodicals through a wholly-owned subsidiary. In France, Italy, Germany, Austria and Brazil, through 50 per cent affiliated companies Maclean-Hunter publishes trade and business periodicals.
Would not our Canadian industry be severely weakened if other countries, specifically the United States, retaliated against the measure we are discussing? Let us face facts. In 1973 Canadians invested more money in foreign countries than was invested by foreigners in Canada. We may not like to see so much of our economy foreign-controlled,
5612

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
but the Canadian investor does not seem to be sufficiently concerned that he wants to buy out foreign investments in his own country.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) has clearly indicated government direction with the Foreign Investment Review Act, a bill which I chaired through committee and which is, I believe, a positive approach to Canadian control. The same ministry issued in 1966 a listing of a dozen guiding principles for good corporate behaviour in Canada. These were for the subsidiaries of foreign companies in Canada. The Reader s Digest Association (Canada) Limited has faithfully lived up to and exceeded those principles.
Let us look for a moment at the clause that requires that issues of a periodical must not be "substantially the same as one or more issues of a foreign periodical. Since the basis of the Digest's world-wide editorial operation is an exchange of articles of international origin and universal interest, a drastic change in the magazine's content and character would be necessary to meet such a requirement. If such a change were made the magazine would no longer be the Digest. Paradoxically, the clause would also inhibit Reader's Digest from circulating Canadian material abroad, since each time a Canadian article is used in an international edition the Canadian edition becomes more "substantially the same." No publisher, and no reader, could support such a grave restriction on magazine's editorial freedom.
I want now, Mr. Speaker, to turn to the consideration of dumping, corporate profit, and its relevance to this bill. In 1974 Reader's Digest paid $1.6 million in Canadian corporate taxes; the company had a net income of less than $1.5 million, re-invested over $500,000, distributed nearly $300,000 to its Canadian shareholders, and exported, although I do not like the term, something over $500,000 to its parent company. That is what we Canadians paid in 1974 for the foreign investment in Canadian plants and equipment and the creation of 1,500 jobs. That is about 8 per cent on investment, or $400 per job. That return, which could surely not be termed excessive, would be substantially less if the parent company charged more for the material it supplies. Thus I suggest that, thanks to the U.S. parent, Canadians are provided with good material at low cost, and benefit at the same time from the corporate taxes levied on the extra profit resulting from this policy. Far from being detrimental this, I suggest, enables us to make a double gain.
The debate on this bill, Mr. Speaker, would not be complete without reference to the cultural aspects. Is Reader's Digest American culture? Is Maclean's Canadian culture? Do we want less of the former and more of the latter? It is not that simple a choice, even if we answer yes to all three questions. We will certainly lose the Canadian content in the American Reader's Digest. Will we buy fewer copies of Newsweek and U.S. News and World Report, or fewer copies of Playboy or Paris Match because they are American-owned or foreign magazines? Incidentally, Air Canada had a full-page advertisement in the April issue of Travel and Leisure, which magazine has a large Canadian circulation. CP Air had a full-page advertisement, and CN also advertised in this same magazine. All that advertising

was paid into American companies and was presumably 100 per cent deductible as an expense.
If I may refer to a recent edition of another U.S. magazine, well over two thirds of the advertising in this magazine applied to products available in Canada. I doubt if the influence on the Canadian consumer goes without recognition.
I would like to quote a few points from articles in magazines and newspapers on this subject which I think are quite pertinent. Martin Murenbeeld, associate professor at the University of Toronto's faculty of management, writing in the Toronto Star said, and I quote:
To run the risk of error in over-simplification I submit that Saturday Night's problems were not lack of advertising revenues, but lack of consumer appeal. Its circulation is poor; business recognizes the facts for what they are and so does not rush at the opportunity to advertise in its pages. Peter Newman and others will no doubt correct me in my belief that audience appeal leads to circulation leads to advertising revenue...
Canadian culture is something that I and many others personally believe in and wish to contribute towards building. This does not, however, mean that we as consumers must be forced to consume Newman's, the Committee for an Independent Canada's, or anyone else's interpretation of what Canadian culture might be.
Mr. W. E. Belliveau, president of Wilshar Advertising Limited, stated in a letter to the Montreal Gazette, and I quote:
How many of your readers know that the Maclean-Hunter group already controls 50 per cent of the Canadian magazine publishing industry, plus radio and television stations? With the loss of Time Canada and Readers' Digest this monopoly could exceed 70 per cent. Are we to trade Time Canada for the monopolistic editorial view of world news that would be supplied by the Maclean-Hunter group?
George Radwanski, writing in the Montreal Gazette, said:
__i{ a publication could attract readers in the absence of these giants-
That is referring to Time and Reader's Digest.
-it could also do so right now. And if it can't, then the problem isn't unfair competition but reader appeal.
In a recent edition of the Ottawa Citizen, there is an editorial which begins as follows:
The regulations governing Time and Reader's Digest to qualify them as Canadian publications, announced by Revenue Minister Ron Bas-ford, are wrong in principle and should be dropped ...
The regulations amount to censorship. It is reasonable to insist on Canadian ownership for a publication to get a Canadian tax break. But it is quite wrong to control content.
In a free society, the contents of magazines and newspapers have to be left to their staffs and subscribers. There may be many publications whose contents the government views with distaste. That's too bad; but that's democracy.
In a recent article, Charles Lynch, who is not always a good friend of the government, said and I quote:
When governments enter the picture, subsidies cannot be far behind, and government subsidies in the field of publication almost invariably are bad news, never more so than when they are coupled with appeals for patriotic support of the publications in question.
My last quote is a comment in an editorial in the New York Times. I think it is of significance. I quote:
Cultural chauvinism, never an attractive feature in the affairs of modern nation states, is particularly objectionable when translated into governmental policy reinforced by economic sanctions ...
May 8, 1975

-we do not see how a democratic country such as Canada could justify in any way the proposed policy of dictating editorial content. Any prescribed quota of Canadian content would be a form of government censorship.
Ultimately, the issue is neither one of percentages nor of the quality of the material. If Canadians feel that they are badly served by foreign cultural imports, they can always respond by producing better publications at home and lending their patronage to foreign magazines more sensitive to Canadian interests. Censorship or news management by law are the wrong answers.
I have tried to outline the reasons why it is my sincere hope that when this bill gets into committee there will be amendments proposed which will rectify some of the injustices I believe are presently being done, particularly to Reader's Digest, a good corporate citizen. That company has tried hard to follow all the directions of the government, and has endeavoured to live up to all the principles that have been established by the government.
In conclusion, as a member who was elected to support this party I shall abide by the majority wishes of this party which have been clearly expressed in caucus, and I shall vote to send this bill to committee. My speech tonight is made with the sincere hope that in committee suitable amendments will be proposed so that the disastrous effects of the legislation as it is presently drafted will not mean the demise of Reader's Digest magazine.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, although I do not have a reputation for offering gratuitous bouquets to members opposite, I would be mistaken if I did not commence my remarks this evening by saying it was a pleasure to be able to sit through the speech of the hon. member for Vaudreuil (Mr. Herbert). His comments were well informed, balanced and very fair. I hope his colleagues on the government side, particularly the Secretary of State (Mr. Faulkner), were attentive to what he had to say and will be responsive to the concerns he expressed.
All of us agree with the goal of trying to give protection and incentive to the Canadian magazine publishing industry. There is no question about the validity of that goal or our desire to see it achieved. While we agree upon the goals we would like to see achieved, we differ sharply on the means of realizing them.
I am an economic nationalist. I believe it is vital that we control our own economy if we are to remain as an autonomous country. It must be obvious that, if the political independence of this country is to be meaningful, we must ensure that decisions as to the future of this country and its people are made here in Canada and not in the corporate board rooms, union head offices, or legislatures of other countries.
Since the days of Macdonald the members of this party have strongly supported the concept that there is a need for the government to act to protect our nationhood and give incentives and protection to Canadian industry to develop here in Canada. However, we have also taken the position that our nationalism must not be destructive. It must not be timid, inward looking, or xenophobic. This is something that distinguishes us most directly from our friends to the left and from some of my colleagues across the way. Very often the comments they make under the guise of nationalism seem to be anti-American or xenophobic. They show some expression of a national inferiori-
Non-Canadian Publications
ty complex. They feel we are incapable of competition on an international scale.
Let us do whatever we can to give protection to Canadian industry and Canadian culture, but let us be careful that when we provide protection for our industries and our countrymen that we do not also deprive our people of the benefits of international competition and the enrichment of our national fabric that comes from interchange with those from other countries. Let us also make sure that we do not simply enshrine mediocrity as a national goal.
Just as I am an economic nationalist, I am a cultural nationalist. There is no purpose in maintaining the mechanisms of political autonomy, or of being masters in our own house in economic affairs if, when we make decisions, we think in the same way as we would think if we belonged to another country. We are responsible for creating an environment in which Canadians are able to live their own lives, to foster dreams which are unique to this country, and to set goals which are good for Canada. It is for this reason that I think we cannot help, as a parliament, being economic nationalists and, as well, cultural nationalists.
I personally support unequivocally the government's plan to disallow advertizing write-offs for television when that advertizing is shown on American television stations and aimed at Canadians. The broadcasting industry in Canada today is threatened in large part by the myopia suffered by Canadian governments and by the ham-fistedness of those governments in dealing with the broadcasting industry. We must give whatever assistance is necessary to prevent limited advertizing dollars from being bled off into the United States, especially when we receive so little in exchange.
The provision contained in the bill before us is a position step in favour of Canadian nationalism and is not one which is designed to penalize anyone or to get at a particular corporation. It is readily defensible, because what the measure is designed to do is to give some degree of protection to the Canadian industry. I do not think the U.S. can very properly object to our desire to keep Canadian dollars from flowing out to American television stations when the products they advertize are American and contain little of Canadian content.
If the actions of the government since the minister has been Secretary of State had been positive and aggressive, if he had taken action to protect our fledgling film industry or to encourage our book-publishing industry and our Canadian magazine industry, I would not view the legislation before us with such suspicion. But that is not the case. The measure we are considering here is a punitive action more fitted to drive American-owned publications out of our country rather than building a strong and vital Canadian publishing industry. This is the one thing which to me, Mr. Speaker, distinguishes the actions of the government and of the Secretary of State. Far from creating, through aggressive positive policy, an environment in which the Canadian publishing industry can prosper and thrive, the government instead has taken merely symbolic

speechtext:
As my hon. friend says-punitive tokenism. Mr. Speaker, make no mistake about it, the passage of the bill before us will not ensure the success of the Canadian publishing industry. Speeches of members on the other side leave the impression that once the Canadian editions of Time and Readers' Digest have been killed we shall move into the golden age of the Canadian magazine industry. Such is not the case. Indeed, there is a significant possibility that the action we are contemplating may be detrimental to the future of the industry in Canada. As Canadian advertizers may well find, it is by no means certain that the remaining periodicals in Canada will give economic access to sufficiently large markets to make advertizing in Canadian periodicals a worthwhile prospect.
We might very well find that because of the absence of a package which would include Time and Readers' Digest to deliver a large market to Canadian advertizers at a very low cost, advertizers will be inclined to shift their advertizing dollars to another medium, resulting in money going from the publishing industry to some other media. Indeed we have only to look at the size of the market reached by Time and Readers' Digest to realize how important they are as part of a package to deliver a large advertizing market to Canadian advertizers.
Readers' Digest is the number one magazine in terms of readership sold in Canada. Time magazine is number four. The survey which was taken on behalf of Readers' Digest by Canadian Facts Ltd. showed, as some previous speakers have mentioned, that probably only about 19 per cent of the revenues which currently go to Time and Readers' Digest will go to Canadian periodicals instead. The government disputes this figure, as did the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie (Mr. Symes) earlier. But no one has offered any evidence to the contrary. It has simply been said that the figure might be wrong, or that it was felt to be wrong. What is striking about the minister's attitude in this regard is his insistence on pushing ahead, forcing the legislation through the House before we have had an adequate opportunity to assess the impact it will have upon the Canadian periodical industry.
I think it worth saying, because it is true and because it is not stated often enough, that Canadians have not been ill-served by Time and Readers' Digest. I listened with interest to the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie decrying the activities of Time magazine. But I do not think we have been ill-served by Time. Yes, that magazine does give an American perspective, but it also provides an extremely good synopsis of world events over the week. I would argue that as well as reading Time we can diversify our reading by following comparable magazines published in other countries, such as The Economists.
Even if the elitists among us-people like the Secretary of State-believe that Canadians have been ill-served and that their needs have not been satisfied by Time and Readers' Digest, I would plead with the government to listen to the voice of the Canadian public. Canadian readers do not believe they have been ill-served. It is apparent
|Mr. Beatty.)
when one considers that Readers' Digest enjoys first place in sales of magazines, and Time is number four, that these periodicals fulfil a need in Canada. The Canadians in my constituency who are regular readers of Readers' Digest and Time do not buy these magazines because they think that they are poor in quality or content; they do so because they find they have needs which are only being met by these publications at the present time.
The minister may argue that it is necessary for Canadian magazines to fill the void. I hope that Canadian magazines will do so. But I would prefer to see Canadian magazines growing up in competition with the magazines we now have available to us, rather than see those two particular magazines destroyed and merely hope that Canadian successors will be good enough to take their place.
With respect to Time magazine I would point out that the reporters working for that publication have distinguished themselves among others in their profession. Although I had some quarrel with the author of an article in which I was mentioned earlier this year, I certainly cannot disagree with the high regard in which reporters of Time are held by their peers. They have often broken stories ahead of their competitors. The Canadian section of the magazine has provided good sources of Canadian news.
I would also stress, as did the hon. member for Vau-dreuil, that Readers' Digest has consistently provided a high degree of Canadian content. Even more important though is that Readers' Digest has presented a vehicle for Canadian writers to get their work read abroad. I am very interested in having Canadian works read in Canada by Canadians. But I think that Canadian artists are first rate and that Canadian writers are first rate. Their work should be seen or read abroad, and we should find mechanisms to encourage the distribution of Canadian work abroad.
There is a great distinction in my mind between the parts of the bill which deal with television and those parts which involve publications. The part of the bill concerned with television is a measure to protect the outflow of Canadian advertising dollars into the United States where those dollars provide few jobs for Canadians and little, if any, Canadian content. The second part of the measure, that dealing with periodicals, is very different. It will cost hundreds of Canadians their jobs. It will eliminate Canadian content currently made available by the two publications affected, and it will remove substantial secondary and tertiary benefits to Canadian suppliers. This is particularly the case in Montreal where many small Canadian businessmen do work for Readers' Digest. It will soon become apparent that many small businessmen will be adversely affected by this part of the bill.
There is no significant and positive step taken under the legislation to provide incentives for Canadian publishers. What it will do is merely redistribute the same number of advertising dollars, and the suggestion is that the number of advertising dollars going to periodicals may in fact diminish.
I am sure that I am just as interested as the Secretary of State in seeing a Canadian news weekly established in this country. We should make no mistake about the reason
May 8, 1975

for the absence of such a Canadian publication at the present time. It is not because of U.S. controlled competitor has co-opted the market in Canada by publishing a Canadian news weekly. The minister stressed the fact that Time magazine is not a Canadian news weekly, and I agree with that. The content is largely American or international, and the percentage of Canadian content is in fact low.
Of course the people who read Time are not paying their 75 cents primarily for the six or seven pages of Canadian news. They are buying it because it provides a perspective on world and American affairs which they cannot get elsewhere.

speechtext:
The hon. member says that they still will be able to buy it, but he misses the distinction I am trying to make. I suggest that if after the Canadian versions of Time and Reader's Digest are killed, as the minister and my friends to my left would like, there is going to be a market for a Canadian news weekly and Canadians will want to buy it then, but that need is not being met at the present time.
My friend suggests that they will be able to buy the American edition of Time even after the Canadian edition is put out of business. Indeed he is correct. This is why people are buying it at the present time. They are buying it largely for United States news. The hon. member is not addressing himself to the fact that the existence of an American news magazine concentrating on American and international content has not co-opted the field if there is a market for a Canadian magazine concentrating on Canadian affairs. Both the Secretary of State and the hon. member for Sault Ste. Marie have made the point that it is the American content we are buying and not the Canadian content. If there is to be that market after this bill passes, there is that market today.
I am not satisfied with the blandishments of the minister who suggests that it is only by driving out Time and Reader's Digest that we are going to get the seed money necessary to establish a new Canadian news weekly and allow it to get going. I simply do not see any evidence for that.
Let us look at who is going to be filling the vacuum if my friends drive Time and Reader's Digest out of business. The vacuum will be very ably and very quickly filled by Maclean-Hunter, a large, wealthy and powerful Canadian publishing giant. I am intrigued to see my hon. friends to my left, who often go on at great lengths to decry large business, supporting a measure which is going to result in the lion's share of the revenue which is currently going to Time and Reader's Digest going into the hands of the corporate giant in Canada in the publishing industry. Let us make no mistake about that.
My friends have talked about the need for a Canadian publishing industry. None of us quarrel with that. Indeed the most dynamic Canadian publishers are not the fat cat corporate giant publishers who are publishing their widely read Canadian publications at the present time. The most innovative ones are the small ones who are publishing on a very marginal footing at present.
Non-Canadian Publications
The advertising revenue which is going to be taken away from Time and Reader's Digest is not going to go to the publishers operating out of church basements; it is going to find its way largely into the hands of the Maclean-Hunter group. I think that instead of talking about punitive action directed against Time and Reader's Digest we should be talking about positive action designed to create an environment in which the Canadian publishers can flourish. That does not mean handouts by the government, it means creating an environment in which they can survive on their own.
I mentioned earlier that the reason why there is not a Canadian news weekly concentrating on Canadian affairs at the present time is not that Time magazine has co-opted the field. If anybody in Canada has the resources and the entrepreneurial skills to fill the void and to satisfy those market needs the Secretary of State is talking about for a Canadian news weekly, that is Maclean-Hunter. It has the money and the entrepreneurial skills to do it at the present time.
While I do not deny that Canadian nationalism is an attractive concept in the Maclean-Hunter corporate board rooms, I also do not take lightly the dedication of that corporation to profit, and that is something that was glossed over by my friends to the left. It is clear they are the ones, and not the struggling Canadian publisher, who will be reaping the most substantial benefits from the government's action.
I personally, as a Conservative and a free enterpriser, would be the last to denounce the ability of the Canadian businessman to make profits. But I do ask that we do not delude ourselves as to who the government beneficiaries in fact will be. They will not be the small businessman, they will be the large corporations.
Another area in which I have strong concern is in the area of interpretation of "Canadian publication" and what would constitute a Canadian publication. The Minister of National Revenue would assign in effect a Canadian content quota on our magazines if they are to receive the critical designation of a Canadian publication. This provision, despite the government's anxious denials, smacks very much of censorship, and it could readily be applied to newspapers which rely substantially upon international wire services for foreign news coverage, or television programs that are taken from foreign networks for events that take place outside our country.
Having sat in parliament for some time and having watched the government perform, it certainly would not be inconceivable to me to see the extension and the invocation of this principle or doctrine against newspapers and television networks in this country that are printing or showing reports about domestic activities or domestic events which the government dislikes. Certainly the case in the United States was that the administration there used its power to intimidate the news media, and used it in a very heavy-handed way.
I believe, as a Conservative who believes in limited government, that where the potential for abuse exists we have a threat to our freedom in a democracy. However much this government protests that it does not intend to abuse its powers, I believe Canadians should regard the government's actions with considerable attention, as

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
indeed they should regard any attempt by its successors to take more power that will affect the freedom of information in a democratic society.
There is no doubt that in this majority parliament, and particularly in respect of this measure on which the government is assured of the support of their ideological cousins to my left, this legislation will in fact be passed. Before long in Canada the Canadian editions of Time and Reader's Digest will disappear, and Canadians will be able to get articles about how Adrienne Clarkson discovered Toronto, and about the Prime Minister's 10 favourite recipes for maple syrup, on a bi-weekly basis instead of on a monthly basis as is the case at the present time.
The government, once it has taken the punitive and symbolic measure it proposes at the present time, will then resume its policy of dynamic paralysis in which the minister allows Canadian culture to struggle alone against governmental indifference, and protest like crazy that somebody else is to blame.
This minister who is so anxious to push this through would have more credibility if he could convince me that the people he is supposed to be serving, the Canadian artistic community, in fact have his backing. Such is not the case. Indeed rumours abound that if the minister fails to get Reader's Digest put out of business, Canadian writers will have a market for a new article to be published in the Canadian edition of Reader's Digest on the Secretary of State, entitled "My most forgettable character".
If it wanted to, the government could move tomorrow to pump new life into our publishing industry. It could reform the operations of our costly and inefficient Post Office so Canadian publishers could get their material promptly and cheaply distributed. If it were serious the government could change the write-offs for advertising in Canadian publications to a positive and substantial tax credit which would provide a positive incentive for Canadian businesses to advertise in our publications. If the government were sincere it could improve distribution of periodicals in Canada to assure Canadians access to Canadian publications.
It has not been the federal government but the government of Ontario that has pioneered in pointing out the breakdown of our periodical distribution industry. This government has sat idly by as the periodical industry in Canada and in Ontario was taken over by a United States corporation, and as Canadian periodicals suffered at the hands of those U.S. distributors. The government would not act.
I started my remarks by mentioning our first Prime Minister, Sir John A. Macdonald. I shall now turn to him because his government differed from this drifting and complacent government. The difference between our present Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and our first Prime Minister is striking. In Macdonald's day we did not have to call conferences to decide what it means to be a Canadian. There was no opposition, except from the predecessors of today's Liberal Party, those who periodically cherish continentalist notions in the desire to preserve our Canadian nationhood. Our artists did not have to try to convince our citizens of our potential to build a society
| Mr. Beatty ]
that would be unique in the world, and an example to other countries. In Macdonald's day Canadianism was not simply a refuge from the world. Canadians defined themselves not in terms of what we were not, but in terms of our goals and dreams for this country.
Today Macdonald's vision has been lost and we are governed by an administration that is characterized by drift and default. In its resources, its geography, its idealism, and industry in respect of its people, this country can be the envy of the world. But if we are to realize our potential it will take new leadership on the treasury benches. The need for new direction in government has never been greater than now.

subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in this debate on Bill C-58 it is my intention to deal with the publications issue and not with the implications with respect to the television industry. My colleagues who have more knowledge in the broadcasting fields will, I am sure, be better able to comment on that aspect.
In my remarks I should like to examine first of all the basic problem the government has sought to solve, and then I should like to deal in some detail with the adverse affects of this proposed legislation. By way of background it should be said that Reader's Digest has had a Canadian edition and a Canadian company for some 32 years, and Time Magazine, perhaps sensing government action, established its Time Canada in Montreal to produce Canadian editions in 1962. These companies have both been good corporate citizens, and we have been bad hosts. The losers, if the government goes ahead, will be the Canadian people generally. Time and Reader's Digest can pull back and go to freer political climes. Someone might ask how that could be.
In his statement on January 23, 1975, the minister, in referring to the 1965 law said that the intent of section 19, in the first place, was to support the Canadian magazine industry, then as now, weakened by the virtual domination of the market by American publications. Did Canadians want the government to support the Canadian magazine industry? We do not know. We do not have the information on which to base that conclusion. If the government thought so, why did it not just take some funds from the general revenue and give them to the industry if it wanted to support the industry? Heaven knows the government has given away money pretty freely, probably in many instances where the recipients may be less worthy.
The minister in that statement continued to say that instead of legislating against the entry of American material, which would have been an interference with the free flow of information and ideas, the framers of section 19 legislated an advantage, or incentive, for actual and potential Canadian magazines. Well, what was the result of the incentive for actual and potential Canadian magazines? Ten years afterward, in 1975, Newsweek, United States News and World Report, and hundreds of other foreign periodicals are selling well in Canada while, curiously, many Canadian publications have had severe financial problems and some have ceased publishing. Perhaps it is time to do something for the Canadian publishing business. What does the government say it will do?
May 8, 1975

It might be interesting for a moment to look at the words of the minister who, in November, said that section 19 will have an advantage or incentive for Canadian magazines. I have paraphrased that slightly, but the intent is there. How often have we heard recently about the special privileges granted Time and Reader's Digest? Even the Canadian Periodical Publishers' Association does not seem to have their story straight. I should like to read a short paragraph from their recent letter dated April 21 this year, in which they say:
We firmly believe that with Time 'Canada' and Reader's Digest competing with Canadian magazines on an equal basis, there will be exciting new work for more writers, designers, photographers, printers, typographers and others in the graphic arts across Canada.
But they have been on an equal basis. The government seeks to alter that by this legislation. The intent was to give special privileges to Canadian magazines, and Time and Reader's Digest for reasons we will examine later were deemed to be Canadian magazines. So, what these two were getting was not treatment that differed from that given to Canadian magazines, but rather was identical treatment.
Probably realizing the contribution of some publications to the well-being of Canada-and do not forget that section 19(2) uses the expression "being edited and printed and published in Canada"-the government decided in 1965 to treat certain non-Canadian publications as if they were Canadian. One can see the government's dilemma. It had pressure on the one hand from its friends in the publishing field in Canada, and pressure on the other hand from its friends in the foreign publishing field.
Let us step back for a moment and take a look at the real effect of Bill C-58. It really will have little effect on Canadian readers. Time and Reader's Digest will still be available to mail subscribers and at newsstands. What it really will do is discriminate against Canadian advertisers. How will it discriminate against Canadian advertisers, one may ask? It will tell the Canadian advertiser that the cost of his advertising in the periodical of his choice will double if the magazine is a non-qualified one. It should be obvious that the Canadian advertiser is unlikely to buy space, for example, in Playboy because the distribution in Canada as a market area is such a small fraction of the total distribution.
That same Canadian advertiser, however, might not want to buy space in a Canadian magazine, even at a much lower cost, because the cost index per reader is too high. But the Canadian advertiser who wants to advertise in a magazine edited, published, and printed in Canada, such as Time Canada and Reader's Digest, is told by the government that the penalty for so doing is the denial of deductibility of this expense. This is discrimination, or censorship by taxation. That is not news to us on this side. Who can not remember the retaliatory action taken by the government against resource producers in the western provinces?
What may not be fully realized by some hon. members is that the advertising that would be placed, for example, in Playboy would be deductible by the advertiser because it would not be, to quote the act, "directed primarily to a market in Canada". So, too, advertisements in Time U.S., Newsweek and other foreign publications would be allowed as a deduction in arriving at net income under the Canadi-
Non-Canadian Publications
an Income Tax Act because it could be directed to a market that was primarily Canadian.
Similarly, Canadian advertisers in say Vancouver or Montreal can deduct the cost of advertising in daily papers in Washington State or New York State. Many businessmen in real estate and other fields use this method of selling their goods or services.
Another aspect of such discrimination will come from the situation where a foreign brand name producer will be able to advertise and deduct the cost in a periodical in Canada. Although not directly involved, the Canadian dealer selling that product will have in effect deducted his share of the cost of this advertisement because it will be hidden in the cost of his product. To put it in simpler terms, a Chevrolet dealer-if we want to take that example-will benefit from advertisements by the U.S. parent company, and the cost of those advertisements will be written off by that Canadian dealer because it is hidden in the cost of his automobiles. Compare this with the Canadian producer of some product who wants to advertise in the same magazine and is refused the right to deduct the cost. Will the "Big Brother" Liberal government help him out when his sales lag or when his expenses are too high? Is this a way for our government to encourage Canadian industry?
I do not want to enter the emotional debate on the value of either Time or Reader's Digest. In fact, I seldom read either of them. May I say, however, that I have received hundreds of letters from readers in my constituency who will be very disappointed and angry if these magazines are forced to leave Canada.
In an article released in March the minister said:
Our intention is not to throw these magazines out of the country.
He glibly continued:
They can conform to the law by meeting the conditions set out in section 19 and become Canadian magazines. Or, like hundreds of other popular foreign magazines which get no special favours from the Government of Canada, they can compete for your attention and advertisers' money. Whichever alternative Time and Reader's Digest accept, Canadians will not be "deprived of the right" to read editions of these magazines.
First of all, commenting on the minister's remarks, if Time and Reader's Digest were to conform to the law by meeting the conditions in section 19, they would cease to be controlled by the present producers, and there is every likelihood that through change they would indeed cease to exist.
Picture, if you can, the Canadian issue of Time or Reader's Digest competing with the U.S. issues. After being stripped of the benefits of the parent organization, the resulting losses would probably call for more government interference to ban, perhaps altogether, foreign publications in Canada.
The minister went on in his remarks in that article to mention the hundreds of other popular foreign magazines which get no special favours from the Government of Canada. It should be pointed out that the advertisers therein are also not penalized by the Canadian government. These foreign magazines are purchased for enjoyment and probably carry little advertising for the Canadi-
May 8, 1975

Non-Canadian Publications
an market, but if they did carry some the cost would be deductible by the advertiser because it is not directed primarily to a market in Canada.
The minister says that Canadians will not be deprived of the right to read editions of these magazines. Certainly I would agree that Time and Reader's Digest will continue to be available on our newsstands and will continue to be mailed to Canadian subscribers, and that Canadians will still read them. But Canadians will be deprived of the Canadian section of Time magazine and they will be deprived of the articles in the Reader's Digest which now appear only in the Canadian edition.
Will Canadians suffer any other losses through this government action? Well, the French edition of Reader's Digest will certainly disappear. I am not sure how the government, which supports so strongly the bilingual program, feels about eliminating the French edition for French speaking Canadians. The advertising that Canadians read in these magazines will be strictly American. Who knows what sales will be lost by Canadian businesses which will have lost this great audience for their advertisements?
What will happen to Canadians presently employed in Vancouver at Evergreen Press, and in Montreal, who edit and print the Canadian editions of these magazines? I am sure that the electors in Vancouver Centre and in West-mount wonder what they were doing when they voted to send two cabinet ministers down here-not just two backbenchers-who would agree to close down these businesses in their very own ridings.
What about the editorial and support staff? Will they be thrown to the wolves as well? And what of the rights of the 550 Canadians who presently own 32 per cent of the Canadian operation of Reader's Digest? They are in a minority position, and the value of their considerable investment has been jeopardized by the actions of the government.
I have not followed the value of Reader's Digest shares on the Toronto Stock Exchange recently, but earlier in the year the stock had fallen from a high of $10.25 to $7, a loss of 30 per cent of the value for those Canadians who invested their hard earned cash in a venture in which they believed.
This Canadian company provides employment for 500 Canadians, and twice that number have supporting jobs outside the company. The Canadian company has a capital of some $8 million, and we have a government that says it wants Canadians to invest in Canada!
One other little heard comment in this argument is the effect that this legislation will have on the Post Office. I am sure the Postmaster General (Mr. Mackasey) has thought of it, but even the Secretary of State agrees that subscribers will still be able to read their Time and Reader's Digest, even if it happens to be the U.S. edition. What is not often mentioned is that the Canadian Post Office will deliver these magazines free of charge even if they are not mailed in Canada.
At present some $3 million is gained by the Canadian Post Office for carrying these magazines from Montreal and Vancouver to subscribers' homes. If they are mailed in the U.S., the Canadian Post Office will still be called upon
|Mr. Clarke (Vancouver Quadra) !
to deliver them, but under international post office agreements will get not one cent for its trouble. Perhaps the Postmaster General should whisper this tale of woe in the ear of the Secretary of State.
I have not dwelt at all on the content requirements which the government wants to impose. The main reason is that it is still quite unclear just what requirements the government has in mind. The Minister of National Revenue has made some reference to the percentage of Canadian content, but nothing has been said about what constitutes Canadian content. Would it be written by a Canadian in a foreign country, or would it be written about a Canadian by a foreigner, or would it be all right if it was written in Canada but by a foreigner about a foreigner?
The Secretary of State says this is not censorship, but he goes on to state what the content must not be. He says his government is not telling Canadians what to read, but it is telling magazines what they can print. I am sure readers in Canada will see this as censorship and as another step in the government's attempt to control the people of Canada.
My colleagues have explained our party's position, which has long been known by Canadians. The PC party favours Canadian ownership of business in Canada. We have long advocated incentives for individuals who are willing to invest in Canada. We are prepared to accept the facts of majority Canadian ownership, but we object most strenuously and cannot agree to government control in publishing content, and we know of no branch of the publishing industry in Canada that would be willing or able to accept this kind of censorship.
