subsubtopic: REMOVAL OF PROVISION ALLOWING DEDUCTION OF EXPENSES FOR ADVERTISING IN NON-CANADIAN PERIODICALS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am really anxious to take part in the debate this evening not solely as a result of the points made by some of my colleagues who spoke on the meaning of Bill C-58, but also to correct some statements reported by newspapers and media on the future activities of the Readers' Digest if Bill C-58 is passed in its present form. However, before taking up again each of those arguments, I would like to remind the House that Bill C-58 is not an isolated bill. For the past five years more particularly, the government has undertaken at the international level, to diversify considerably the traditional markets of Canada. We have noted at the international level that our economy is much too dependent on the American market and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce has made considerable efforts to send missions and open offices in various countries, more especially in Latin America and the Middle East.
The Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Gillespie) stated this week during the consideration of his estimates that our trade with countries such as Venezuela had more than doubled during the past year. We have registered a large increase as far as Iran and Saudi Arabia are concerned.
On the national level, the government has set as its highest priority the passage in two steps of a legislation meant to enable the Canadian people to make a fair and complete contribution to the definition of our economic destiny. The policy presently implemented by the Foreign Investment Review Agency which has operated for the past year has shown that the need was becoming more and
Non-Canadian Publications
more urgent and that without an immediate intervention, we would very shortly be running the risk of merely becoming an extension of the neighbouring market. The second stage of this legislation aiming to control new foreign investments has been long overdue. This morning, newspapers reported that the Quebec government has revealed the guidelines of its control policy on foreign investment. It is not without reason that one of the major sectors that will be subjected to the provincial agency will be the social and cultural sector, and for obvious reasons in the case of the province of Quebec.
In the cultural field, and particularly in the field of publishing, the federal government has taken many steps over the last three years. I listened this afternoon to the opposition spokesman who read a list of suggestions that he qualified as positive ones in order to improve the publishing industry in Canada. I should like to remind him that several of his suggestions have already been implemented by the federal government. On the one hand, the federal government directed its efforts to the consideration of amendments to the Foreign Investment Review Act in such a way as to include publishing firms, and also to allow the Review Agency to consider and refuse, as the case may be, the expansion in Canada of foreign-con-trolled publishing firms. Bill C-58, therefore, is not an isolated measure. On the other hand, the Canadian publishing industry support program has been substantially increased in the last year. More than $1,500,000 have been earmarked for this program and during the year 1972-73, more than 400 books have been published and put on the Canadian market.
The hon. member of the opposition also pointed out the need to put publications on the Canadian market in federal buildings. Rules were passed under which adequate quantities of Canadian publications, books and magazines, should be made available to the public in bookshops located in federal buildings.
Finally, direct financial assistance was given owners of bookshops to enable them to open shops not only in the capitals and large centres but also in smaller towns which do not now have access to that kind of service.
Mr. Speaker, I listened closely to my colleagues who brandished the spectre of censorship when Canadian content in the field of publication was discussed. I always find an element of demagoguery in that argument, especially considering the regulations passed by the CRTC in the last few years which are intended to encourage broadcaster now operating in Canada to ensure a Canadian content of at least 60 per cent.
I cannot recall that since those regulations are enforced there have been fears of censorship or protests on the part of the Canadian public about their timeliness. In fact, from the comments I have heard, I note that the public has wondered precisely why the government did not take those steps sooner. Which does not mean, Mr. Speaker, that Canadian television, whether private or public, exercises a censorship or even an embargo against foreign artists or producers or foreign films, which is detrimental to the freedom of which our country has always been a champion.

May 8, 1975
Non-Canadian Publications
Mr. Speaker, I feel that a country like Canada, whose economy rests on a relatively limited foundation, whose population is scattered over a territory as vast as that of our neighbours to the south, must take positive steps to ensure not only that it keeps its national identity, but especially that it develop in an atmosphere of freedom.
Mr. Speaker, Bill C-58 is part of this general context, and I felt I should recall its outline because I am convinced it is not an isolated gesture but rather one of many elements of the total concept of a cultural policy which it is intended to be as dynamic in the publishing sector as in the film industry and the performing arts. I do not have to recall that the Income Tax Act was amended in order to enable investors who are mainly interested in the movie industry to have appropriate abatements, in order to facilitate and to induce Canadian investments into this industry which must be developed. When we think that a country like Canada is neighbour to an international monopoly at the level of movie production, we cannot help but hope that such legislation will be passed.
When we try to apply the same objectives to the publishing industry, we realize, Mr. Speaker, that one of the first things to do is precisely to define a context in which Canadian publications will be preferred by Canadians.
With Bill C-58, the government does not seek to eliminate Time or the Reader's Digest or the Selection du Reader's Digest. The government has no right to decide on the relevance of one of these magazines when they comply with the laws of public order and security, Mr. Speaker. The responsibility of the government lays more in ensuring that Canadian publications receive adequate treatment and that, if privileges are to be given, they are given first to Canadian publications.
In the course of the discussions, the spectre of the disappearance of the Reader's Digest has also been raised. Mr. Speaker, this argument does not take into account the economic basis of this firm. As a matter of fact, since 1958, this firm has been engaged in the sale of all kinds of products, because it had a very expanded list of customers, perhaps one of the longest in Canada. It engaged in the sale of records, books, publications, reference material which represent more than 58.6 percent of its aggregate turnover for 1974.
Of the $30 million turnover of Reader's Digest in 1974, more than $18 million came from the sale of articles which have nothing to do with the publishing of the Reader's Digest, the Selection du Reader's Digest. That means that from 1958 to 1968, the corporation significantly diversified its economic basis in such a way that the portion of the revenue it draws from the sale of the magazine represents only $6 million, that is 20.5 per cent of the gross revenue of the corporation.
It is therefore erroneous to say or to maintain that this corporation would inevitably go bankrupt if it had to stop publishing the magazine tomorrow. In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, the company made a wise decision in 1958 when it diversified its economic basis, as most dynamic entre-prises in Canada do, to protect themselves against market instability. I do not think, Mr. Speaker, that even if Reader's Digest stopped being published, the company would be driven out of business on the Canadian market. Indeed, if
it stopped publishing these two magazines completely, it would only lose 13 per cent of its total gross revenues.
I think, Mr. Speaker, that to tell employees and lead them to fear that they would lose their jobs if the magazine was no longer published is to use for demagogic purposes a staff that has always served this entreprise well. And I think that since the federal government is also committed to assist printers, we must keep in mind that the Department of Supply and Services gives contracts to small printing companies for amounts five times higher than those the Reader's Digest receives for the publishing of its two magazines.
The Canadian government is aware that it must help small publishing and printing companies, and I think, Mr. Speaker, that if the government must review its policy, it is precisely in order to decentralize the granting of government contracts, much more than to force small publishers out of business in remote areas, be they in Eastern or in Western Canada.
Through Bill C-58, Mr. Speaker, the government is in fact seeking three things which are quite legitimate. First of all, the government wants a Canadian control over the content of these two periodicals. How can we allow a firm to benefit from tax privileges when it holds a permit under which it can veto the content of articles to be published for the Canadian market? What we are asking this firm is to change its charter so that the control over the content of its publications be brought back to Canada. I do not feel it is too much to ask a multinational in 1975 to surrender this control to the country where it is operating at a profit and has tax privileges.
The second condition the government imposes on Reader's Digest and Time Magazine is that of the Canadian content. Mr. Speaker, I must say that as a Francophone, I was extremely sorry to hear that the translation into French of Reader's Digest is being done in France and not in the province of Quebec. I feel that for the past five years, this government has made great efforts, with the support of the House to promote the development of bilingualism in Canada. The government has even set up a program to transfer to the provinces large amounts of money in order to ensure that services are provided in both official languages.
To leave to France the translation into French of the Reader's Digest, that is a kind of colonialism which the Canadian government has rejected several years ago. Mr. Speaker, I hope, if the Selection du Reader's Digest is to continue to be published in Canada, there will be enough qualified French speaking Quebequers to ensure the French translation of the articles.
I think it would be quite easy to define, on the basis of the CRTC experience, a content that would take into account the Canadian identity, at the level of either the author or the subject matter or through the way a foreign author could be associated with the magazine. I think, Mr. Speaker, that we have set with CRTC a precedent which still leaves room for a Canadian content in that magazine.
Mr. Speaker, when we talk about foreign ownership, and I will end with that point, I think the Foreign Investment Agency has shown with more necessity that to ask today a corporation to offer Canadians the ownership of its capital

May 8, 1975

is a perfectly legitimate request within the government policy. Therefore, Mr. Speaker, I hope I will have the privilege, during the committee stage, to put these arguments forward again, so that the real elements of the problem and not only the ghost of veto or loss of jobs will be out in the open.
A motion to adjourn the House under Standing Order 40 deemed to have been moved.

subtopic: HISTORIC SITES-ENTRANCE FEE TO LOWER FORT GARRY- REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
HISTORIC SITES-ENTRANCE FEE TO LOWER FORT GARRY- REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, during question period this afternoon I asked the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Buchanan) to take another look at the question of charging an admission fee to get into Lower Fort Garry which is located on the Red River, about 18 miles or so north of the city of Winnipeg. This afternoon, in asking my question for the seventh or eighth time, I asked the minister to look at this matter with a sense of history.
The fact is, Sir, that for many years Lower Fort Garry was privately owned and operated. It was the preserve of an elite club and the only way you could get into the fort was by belonging to the club or by being a friend of a member of that club. Some of us thought this was unfortunate, for the result was that an historic site in Manitoba was effectively closed to the general public. The day came when the federal government took it over and made it available for the public, which was to be admitted free of charge. We in Manitoba, thought this was a good idea. That regime lasted for quite a few years.
Recently the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development imposed an admission or entrance fee to Lower Fort Garry. In response to the appeals that some of us made, the minister made an adjustment, but it did not amount to much. The fee is still $2 for an adult, and 50 cents for a child. At the beginning there was a family fee of $5, but that has been reduced to $4. That is not much; actually in Manitoba it is felt to be a bit of an insult. Another adjustment was the provision for an annual family pass for $10, which really is meaningless.
I make the point that Lower Fort Garry is not a picnic ground, is not a national park like Banff, is not like Lake Louise or Cape Breton Highlands; you do not travel around in it and camp, and so on. It is an historic site, something one goes to see, not because of the beauty of the place, although it is an attractive spot, but because of an interest in history. One goes in there to see the relics of a bygone century and to feel some of the history of Manitoba, some of the history of western Canada. We, in Manito-
Adjournrnent Debate
ba, think it is most unfortunate and most unwise for the government to dampen interest in that historic site by imposing this fee.
All of us who come from the province of Manitoba know that the opposition to this fee is widespread. Organizations right across the spectrum-religious, political, economic and others-feel that this is an unfair practice on the part of the federal government. I hope that even yet the department will go back to the practice of a number of years and charge no fee at all; or, if there must be a fee, let it be a very minimal one indeed. The idea of a family pass for $10 a year or special fee for tour groups, students, and so on, really does not meet the situation. I earnestly hope that the appeal we are making will be considered.
I was interested this afternoon to note a sheer coincidence, because that is what it was. Immediately after my question to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development came the question of the hon. member for Marquette (Mr. Stewart), which he directed to the Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs (Mr. Ouellet), in which he asked if it was not time to prosecute the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development for such an exorbitant increase in its fees. He, of course, was referring to Riding Mountain national park where the increase was 500 per cent or 1,000 per cent. Of course I am referring to a case where the increase is infinity, from zero to the figures to which I just referred.

speechtext: Just like the Rideau Canal.

subtopic: HISTORIC SITES-ENTRANCE FEE TO LOWER FORT GARRY- REQUEST FOR RECONSIDERATION
speechtext:
No doubt there will be complaints about that; I hope there will be. But I make the point that the Rideau Canal is something on which one travels. One uses a boat to go on the canal. That is not the case with Lower Fort Garry. There is attached to it a kind of park with a golf course and so on. But it is not a campground, a place where you stay overnight. Nor is it a place you drive around. You go there to see the fort, the walls, gun holes, the boats and the ancient equipment in the museum.
If you start charging people to go to a place like that, what will be next? Are we going to charge people to get into any kind of library, art gallery or museum? Maybe we should start charging people to come into the galleries of this House of Commons. We might retire the national debt. Of course we might go broke.

We do not charge people to get into the Peace Tower or the rotunda of this building. We want people to come here. We want them to have a sense of history. We want them to visit Lower Fort Garry. It is a foolish policy to try to pay for the operation of it by these fees. I waved goodbye to the Minister of Indian Affairs when he left at ten o'clock, for his answers have not been satisfactory. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all I can say to the hon. member is that the people of western Canada have paid for the use of parks for 40 years. Some of the people in eastern Canada are now beginning to discover the virtue of paying for parks.
Parks Canada has recently undergone a period of expansion which included increasing the number of national parks and national historic parks and sites, as well as taking over operation of historic canals in Ontario, Quebec and Nova Scotia which are part of the newly created ARC branch, Agreements for Recreation and Conservation.
Although the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) has raised the issue of entrance fees at Lower Fort Garry, I would like to note there has been a growing demand for parks facilities. I would like to lead into some of the background of the decisions about which he speaks.
Last year there were more than 21 million visitors to parks across Canada, almost double that of ten years earlier. Parks Canada has been striving to meet this demand with increased facilities. However, in many instances this expansion has been at the expense of the older, established parks in the system which have not had the general servicing they once enjoyed due to the pressing priority of funding to the newer park areas.
To meet this growing challenge, and subject to parliamentary approval, Parks Canada will undertake a $376 million development program during the next five years.

subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN REGIONAL PAY RATES IN DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES
PUBLIC SERVICE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN REGIONAL PAY RATES IN DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to pursue my question of April 28 concerning regional rates of pay in Canada for federal employees, a subject which is causing understandable concern and unrest among citizens who are affected.
I have tried to be reasonable in presenting the case but it is impossible for me to believe there can be any justification for the present differences in pay rates, nor can I be persuaded that the policy fits in with what are supposed to be our national goals-equality of opportunity, an end to regional disparity, and the maintenance of human decency. It is evidently the policy of the government not only to maintain the discrepancy in regional rates but to expand the present practice.
The whole basis upon which regional pay rates are established is that it costs less to live in certain parts of the country. However, in present conditions this contention is out of date, and this being the case the whole trend should be reversed. Rather than pay rates in Newfoundland, for example, being lowest and those in Vancouver being the highest, the reverse should be true at a time when the cost of living in Newfoundland is the highest in Canada. So the present policy is unfair, as well as lacking in sense. Not only is it contradictory to the objective of the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, which is to overcome regional disparity; it is preventing the achievement of that goal. As I have indicated, the Treasury Board is operating on the basis of discrimination against federal employees in the Atlantic region.
What the government is really saying is that federal firefighters are not as capable of protecting an aircraft if, God forbid, one burns in Newfoundland as if it burns in Montreal, Toronto, Winnipeg or Vancouver. It is saying that the Canadian passenger is less a Canadian after he leaves Montreal to fly east. What it is really saying is that the federal nurse who serves the veterans in Camp Hill, Halifax, or in the veterans' wing in St. John's, Newfoundland, is treating her patients with less care than that received by patients in other parts of Canada. What it is really saying is that the heavy equipment operator cannot perform his duties as a snow cleaner, for example, in Newfoundland as well as those who work in other parts of the country, or that the safety factor is of less importance.
I should like the minister to explain to me how, to give one example, a company which has contracted to manage the Deer Lake Airport can pay higher salaries to its employees than the Ministry of Transport under regional pay rates. How can I give an answer to the secretary-treasurer of a component of the Public Service Alliance when he expresses the feeling of his membership that Treasury Board is adamant in trying to destroy the national pay structure for federal firefighter as well as other groups? How can I explain to a heavy equipment operator why, after he has worked for ten years, at $3.54 an hour, he is not deserving of equality in pay rates although his son,

May 8, 1975

working between school terms, can earn as much as he earns by working as a carpenter's helper?
Something has to be wrong, and while I appreciate the difficulties experienced by government it is ridiculous that qualified personnel in the Public Service should be classified as lesser Canadians in certain parts of our country though they perform duties equal to those carried out in other parts of the nation. I hope the minister will recognize the inequity which exists, and correct it in the interest of all that is right for Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. Jean Chretien (President of Treasury Board):
subtopic: PUBLIC SERVICE-SUGGESTED INCREASE IN REGIONAL PAY RATES IN DISADVANTAGED PROVINCES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the problem which the hon. member has raised is not an easy one. It is not, of course, a question of justice or injustice. I think we have to look at two Sides of the question. The government wants to be equitable in its treatment of its employees, and pay rates comparable with those paid outside the service to those in similar occupations.
The other day I was talking with the provincial Minister of Finance for the New Brunswick government. He was complaining that some of our civil servants are too well paid and that we are raiding his civil service because he cannot pay them that much. You can appreciate the problem.
Let us take the case of a secretary, a plumber or a carpenter, or some such occupation. We want to pay these people the prevailing rate in the area. Because of our potential we could pay higher rates but we would then create a lot of pressure on the local economy. Really good regional rates will take into account the cost of living in the regions.
This is not a question of discriminating. We want to be absolutely neutral on regional rates. We want to pay our employees at the same level as the municipalities, provinces, and private sectors in the area or locality are paying. This is just fair to the various regions. If we pay the national level in a little village or a town, everyone will want the same level, and some of the local governments cannot afford this.
I have received complaints about this. Of course it depends very much on the kind of occupation involved. We are not in competition for local manpower in the various areas. Take the postal workers, for example. We are not competing with another system so we pay them at the national rate. When we are competing with the locality for local manpower we want to be fair to the local economy. This is something we are debating and negotiating with the unions in some areas.
We saw an example of this last year in regard to the firefighters working at Vancouver. Because they have a national rate they were getting $2 less than the firefighters working for the city of Vancouver. I felt it was unfair, and my predecessor was willing to give them the prevailing rate for firefighters in Vancouver. The union said no, they wanted the national rate. So the thing works both ways.
When we are in competition we have to make sure our employees are as well paid as the local people, but not too well paid in relation to them, because soon after that the local people complain that they are being raided by the

federal civil service. They complain that we are taking away their best manpower by paying them at higher rates.

THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INFLATION-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on April 18 in reply to a question put by me concerning what steps the government was taking to ensure that the Canadian dollar would not be allowed to drift down and remain at the 96-cents to 98-cents level in terms of the United States dollar, the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) said:
-it is Canadian policy that the dollar respond to market forces and that any intervention by the governor of the bank would be only to assure that the float does not have any ... dirt in it.
The Prime Minister was not being candid with the Canadian people in that statement. To suggest it is Canadian policy that the dollar should respond to market forces and any intervention by the government is only to ensure that the float does not have any dirt in it, is totally misleading.
The government guides the market and, as it guides it, the government influences the exchange rate of our dollar with other currencies, in particular that of the United States. While the Prime Minister was misleading parliament with that answer he gave to my question Wood Gundy was reporting.
We expect the authorities will continue to support the dollar if need be by continuing to run down reserves. The Canadian dollar could easily fall to the 97-cent level, in terms of the U.S. dollar, in the next few months.
We have to take a look at the government's policy and what it is costing the Canadian public. The four point drop in the Canadian dollar in terms of inflation, as a result of higher import costs to Canadians, is going to add approximately 1 per cent to the level of inflation in this country.
The other factor I believe we should realize in this House is that by following a high interest level in this country the government in fact is insisting for example that those who have mortgages, will have to carry the cost of the national deficit on their backs. Translated into terms that are perhaps understandable to all of us in this House, I would point out that the government in requiring present domestic mortgage rates-and let there be no doubt that it is government policy to have a mortgage rate of 10 3A per cent in this country-is subjecting a man who has a $40,000 mortgage to an extra cost of $875 a year compared to the American level of 8 per cent for the same mortgage. If this rate is maintained for a full 25 years of amortization, the cost to a Canadian is $21,861.
The fact is that the Prime Minister knows that through the Bank of Canada he is influencing mortgage rates in this country, and in turn is causing the average home owner to pay a severe penalty for the trade deficit we are now running with the rest of the world.

May 8, 1975
Adjournment Debate
Speaking about the trade deficit, I think the government must answer-and I would hope it would answer at an early date in this House-for the sad unproductivity we have, so far as our unit costs in the world are concerned. The Citibank in its April 1975, bulletin suggested a comparison of labour costs in the various countries as against the United States.
It is interesting to note that when the Minister of Finance (Mr. Turner) took over in 1970 hourly compensation in Canada was 75 per cent of that in the United States. In 1974 it had gone up to 86 per cent. The output per man hour in 1970 was 88 per cent. In the past year it actually went down to 87 per cent. The staggering thing is that we have lost entirely the unit labour advantage we had in 1970. In 1970 it was 85 per cent of the American while today it is 99 per cent. That is the situation into which the Minister of Finance has got us. The Minister of Finance now suggests there is a new system called recycling. He is running around the world trying to get money to cover the trade deficit which is accruing at an alarming rate.
Let us face the facts. What he is suggesting is that through recycling he will pile debt on debt in this country. If you cycle far enough there is no surer way to put this country in a disastrous situation, and I think the Minister of Finance, instead of being candid with the Prime Minister, and the Prime Minister instead of being candid with us, are not facing the facts. We have lost our competitive position in the world. We are running up, according to Industry, Trade and Commerce figures given us in committee only two nights ago, a decline of 7 per cent in current volume terms in our trade with the rest of the world. A staggering deficit is coming. I suggest it is government policy deliberately to keep domestic interest rates high in this country in order that we can attract foreign funds through this process called recycling. That is, they will try to get back some of the money that is being lost through the trade deficit with other nations at a higher interest cost.
One of the groups in this country that is going to pay dearly for this government policy is made up of the mortgage holders. As I have stated, the total cost on an annual individual basis is almost $800. I believe this warrants a proper answer from the Prime Minister. I think that the government must be more candid with the Canadian public on what exactly is its policy.

speakeroldname: Mr. Jack Cullen (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Finance):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance
subtopic: THE CANADIAN ECONOMY-INFLATION-GOVERNMENT POLICY ON RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN CANADIAN AND UNITED STATES DOLLAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when one listens to the conclusions reached by the hon. member through his convoluted reasoning, the word that comes readily to mind is claptrap.
The Canadian dollar has fallen somewhat in recent months. But I might point out that its value is still high relative to its level in recent years. Indeed, since observance of the par value of $92.5 U.S. cents was suspended on May 30, 1970, the Canadian dollar has risen by more than 5 per cent.
The advantages and disadvantages of a changing exchange rate cut both ways. While a decline in the value of the Canadian dollar adds to the cost of our imports, it also provides a competitive edge to our exporting industries. The converse is true when the dollar rises, of course. Generally, we cannot label movements in the Canadian dollar as unambiguously beneficial or harmful for our economy.
In any event, as the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) pointed out on April 18, it is the policy of the government to let the value of the Canadian dollar be determined by market forces. Intervention by the government is confined to maintaining orderly market conditions, that is, to preventing erratic movements in the exchange rate. In fact Canada's official international reserves have fallen since May, 1974, when the Canadian dollar reached a peak of more than U.S. $1.04, by more than U.S. $400 million. This drop reflects the stabilizing role intervention has performed and does not run counter to our "clean float" policy.
Movements in the value of the Canadian dollar reflect changes in the many components of the balance of international payments. Whether the dollar goes up or down in any given period of time depends on whether the balance of changes leads to a greater or lesser net demand for Canadian dollars.
In the past year we have seen a substantial deterioration in the balance of current account, that is, in the value of goods and services we sell to non-residents less the amount we buy from them. In 1974 the deterioration amounted to almost $1.5 billion. Preliminary numbers for 1975 suggests some further decline has occurred this year. These developments in the current account reflect the weakness which prevades the economies of our major trading partners. This has kept our exports down. On the other hand, Canadian imports have been sustained in line with the relatively favourable conditions we have experienced here at home.
Whether or not such developments cause a currency to decline depends on the concomitant movements in the capital account, that is, the extent to which net borrowing from non-residents increases sufficiently to finance the current account decline. In 1974 net capital inflows into Canada increased by more than enough to finance our growing current account deficit. Nor do we anticipate any problem financing our net imports in 1975.
